It is said: "So-and-so was *shaqiya* with such-and-such" when he tired because of it and did not attain his aim.

One of them: he feared that they would inherit from him. Said by Ibn ʿAbbās. [p. 208]

If an objector objects and says: how is it permissible for a prophet to begrudge his kinsmen the rights that are obligatory for them after his death?

As for the *hā*, they all said it is from His name *al-Hādī* (the Guide), except al-Qurazī, who said it is from His name *Allāh*. As for the *yā*, there are three opinions: one: it is from *Ḥakīm* (the Wise). Two: from *Raḥīm* (the Merciful). Three: from *Amīn* (the Trustworthy). Saʿīd ibn Jubayr related these three opinions from Ibn ʿAbbās. As for the *ʿayn*, there are four opinions: one: it is from *ʿAlīm* (the All-Knowing). Two: from *ʿĀlim* (the Knower). As for the *ṣād*, there are three opinions: one: it is from *Ṣādiq* (the Truthful). Two: from *Ṣadūq* (the Very Truthful); Saʿīd [ibn Jubayr] related both of these from Ibn ʿAbbās as well. One: so that it would be far from ostentation (*riyāʾ*); said by Ibn Jurayj.

This story indicates that it is recommended to make supplication in secret, and from it is the ḥadīth: "Indeed, you do not call upon one who is deaf."

It means: the white hair spread through it as the light of fire spreads through firewood, and this is among the finest metaphors. ﴿And I have never been, in my supplication to You, my Lord, unblessed﴾; that is: in my supplication to You. ﴿Unblessed (*shaqiyyan*)﴾: that is, I have never been one who tires himself with supplication and then is disappointed; for You have accustomed me to being answered. It is said: "So-and-so was *shaqiya* with such-and-such" when he tired because of it and did not attain his aim.

Regarding what he feared for them concerning it, there are two opinions:

One of them: he feared that they would inherit from him. Said by Ibn ʿAbbās. [p. 208]

If an objector objects and says: how is it permissible for a prophet to begrudge his kinsmen the rights that are obligatory for them after his death?

Concerning this there are two answers. One: since he was a prophet, and a prophet is not inherited from, he feared that they would inherit his property and take what was not lawful for them. I say: the explanation of this is that his property must be managed even if it were not an inheritance, so he loved that his son should manage it.

Ibn al-Jawzi, Zad al-Masir, on Surah Maryam, verses 7–11:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good tidings﴾. In the speech there is an ellipsis (idmar); its estimated sense is: so Allah answered him, and He said: ﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good tidings﴾. Hamza recited (nubashshiruka) with the lightened form (takhfif). We have explained this in (Al 'Imran: 39).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We have not made for him before [this] any namesake﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions:

The first: No one had been named Yahya before him. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by 'Ikrima, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, and most of the scholars.

If an objector says: What is the merit in a name that no one had borne before him, when we see many names that were not preceded? The answer: the aspect of excellence is that Allah, the Exalted, Himself undertook his naming and did not leave that to his parents, so He named him with a name that had not been borne before.

The second: The barren women had not borne a child like him. This was related by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas. According to this, the meaning is: We have not made for him a counterpart (nazir).

The third: We have not made for him before a like and a similar (mithl wa shabah). This was said by Mujahid. According to this, the absence of similarity is in respect of the fact that he did not disobey and did not intend disobedience.

What follows this is explained in (Al 'Imran: 39), up to His saying: ﴿And my wife has been barren﴾.

Concerning the meaning of "kanat" (was) there are two opinions:

The first: It is an emphasis of the speech, so the meaning is: "and she is barren," like His saying: ﴿You were the best nation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]; that is, "you are."

The second: That she had been barren since she came into existence, and that this had not newly occurred to her. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both, and he preferred the first.

**(p-٢١٣)** Allah's words: ﴿O Yahya﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: We bestowed Yahya upon him, and We said to him: "O Yahya." ﴿Take the Book﴾, meaning the Torah, and he was commanded to hold fast to it. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is: accept all the Books of Allah, believing in them and acting upon their rulings. We have explained the meaning of His words "with strength" in (al-Baqarah: 63).

Allah's words: ﴿And We gave him judgment﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

The first is that it is understanding, said by Mujahid. The second is intellect, said by al-Hasan and Ikrimah. The third is knowledge, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The fourth is memorizing the Torah and knowing it, said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. We have expanded on this in the commentary on Surah (Yusuf: 22). Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Whoever recites the Qur'an before reaching puberty is among those who were given judgment while still a child."

As for His words ﴿as a child﴾, there are two opinions regarding his age on the day he was given judgment:

One is that he was seven years old, narrated by Ibn Abbas from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The other is that he was three years old, said by Qatadah and Muqatil.

Allah's words: ﴿and compassion from Us﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, and We gave him compassion. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is: and We made him compassion for the people of his time.

Regarding *hanan* (compassion) there are six opinions:

The first is that it is mercy, narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. This was also said by al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Farra', and Abu Ubaydah, who recited:

*"Show compassion to me, may the Sovereign guide you, for every station has its speech."*

**(p-٢١٤)** He said: and it is most commonly used in speech in the dual form. Tarafah said:

*"O Abu Mundhir, you have spent us out; so spare some of us. Hananayka (both your compassions); some evil is easier than other evil."*

Ibn Qutaybah said: from this one says "tahannana 'alayya" (show compassion to me), and its origin is from the yearning of a she-camel for her young. Ibn al-Anbari said: the lexicographers have not disagreed that *hanan* means mercy, and the meaning is: We did that out of mercy to his parents and as purification for him.

The second is that it is compassion from his Lord toward him, said by Mujahid. The third is that it is gentleness, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The fourth is blessing, also reported from Ibn Jubayr. The fifth is love, said by Ikrimah and Ibn Zayd. The sixth is veneration, said by Ata' ibn Abi Rabah.

Regarding His words ﴿and purity﴾ there are four opinions:

The first is that it is righteous deeds, said by al-Dahhak and Qatadah.

The second is that *zakah* means charity, so the meaning is that Allah made him a charity with which he gave to his parents, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third is that *zakah* means purification, said by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth is that *zakah* means increase, so the meaning is: We gave him an increase in goodness beyond what has been described and mentioned, said by Ibn al-Anbari.

Allah's words: ﴿and he was pious﴾. Ibn Abbas said: I made him one who fears Me, not associating anyone else with Me.

Allah's words: ﴿and dutiful to his parents﴾; that is, We made him dutiful to his parents. *Barr* has the meaning of *barr* (dutiful one), and the meaning is: gentle with them and good to them. *'Asiyy* has the meaning of *'asi* (disobedient). We have explained the meaning of *jabbar* in (Hud: 59).

**(p-٢١٥)** Allah's words: ﴿and peace be upon him﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One is that it is the well-known peace from Allah. Ata' said: "Peace be upon him from Me on these days." This is the choice of Abu Sulayman.

The other is that it means safety, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

If it is asked: how did He specify greeting him with peace on "days," when he may be born at night and die at night?

The answer is that by "day" is meant a period and a time, as we explained in His words: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

Ibn Abbas said: "And peace be upon him the day he was born." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: Yahya and Isa met, and Yahya said to Isa: "You are better than me." Isa said to Yahya: "Rather, you are better than me; Allah has sent peace upon you, and I have sent peace upon myself." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same, except that he said: "Allah has praised you, and I have praised myself." Sufyan ibn Uyaynah said: A person is most lonely in three situations: the day he is born, when he sees himself coming out of what he was in; the day he dies, when he sees people he had not seen; and the day he is raised, when he sees himself in a gathering he has never seen. Allah specified Yahya in these with honor and safety in the three situations.

**The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 19, verses 16–21**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And mention in the Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿Mary, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place.﴾ Abu Ubayda said: she withdrew and separated herself. ﴿A place in the east﴾ means one lying toward the east, and among the Arabs the eastern direction is better than the western.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So she took a screen apart from them﴾, meaning from her people, ﴿a screen (hijab)﴾, that is, a cover and a barrier. There are three opinions on this:

The first: she set up a curtain. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas.

The second: the sun shielded her so that none of them could see her, and Allah concealed her by this means. This meaning is also reported from Ibn Abbas.

The third: she took a barrier of walls. This was said by al-Suddi, from his teachers.

Regarding the reason for her seclusion from them, there are two opinions:

One: she withdrew in order to purify herself from menstruation and comb her hair. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: to delouse her head. This was said by Ata'.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So We sent to her Our Ruh﴾. It is Jibril according to the view of the majority (jumhur, the bulk of the scholars). Ibn al-Anbari said: the companion of Our Ruh, and he is Jibril. The word ar-ruh (الرُّوحُ) carries the meaning of "spirit" and "joy." Then the letter ra is vowelled with a damma to affirm the pattern of the noun and to rule out the pattern of the verbal noun (masdar). It is also permissible that by ar-ruh is meant here the revelation, and Jibril is the bearer of revelation.

Regarding the time of his coming to her, there are three opinions:

(p-217) The first: while she was bathing. The second: after she had finished and put on her garments. The third: after she had entered her house. It has also been said that the intended ar-ruh here is the spirit from which Isa was created. This was related by az-Zajjaj and al-Mawardi, and it is the substance of the statement of Ubayy ibn Ka'b which we will mention at the words: (so she conceived him). Ibn al-Anbari said: but this is distant, because of His saying: ﴿So he presented himself to her as a man of complete form﴾, and the meaning is that he appeared to her in the form of a man of perfect build. Ibn Abbas said: he came to her in the form of a young man with a white face, with curly hair, when his moustache had just begun to grow. Abu Nuhayk recited: (fa-arsalna ilayha rawhana), with a fatha on the ra of ar-ruh (رَوْحَنا).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are fearing (taqiyyan)."﴾ The meaning is: if you fear Allah, you will desist because of my seeking refuge in Him from you. This is the view of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqin). It is related from Ibn Abbas that in her time there was a man named Taqiyy, who was a sinner, and she thought him to be that man. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari and al-Mawardi. In the reading of Ali, peace be upon him, Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Raja': (illa an takuna taqiyyan), "unless you are a God-fearing person."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said, "I am only a messenger of your Lord"﴾, that is: so do not fear. Others said: he did not say (bughyatan), because it is diverted from its original form, and it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active). The meaning of the verse is: I have no husband, and I am not an adulteress, and a child comes only from one of these two sources.
