**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 19, verses 22–26 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she conceived him﴾, meaning Jesus.

There are two views on how she conceived him:

One: Gabriel blew into the opening of her garment, and the conception continued in her. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Suddi said: He blew into the opening of her shift, which was slit at the front, and the breath entered her chest, and she conceived at that moment.

The second: The one who addressed her is the one who conceived him, and he entered through her mouth. This was said by Ubayy ibn Ka'b. [p. 219]

On the duration of her pregnancy there are seven views:

First: She gave birth as soon as she conceived. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and the meaning is that her pregnancy was not prolonged, not that she gave birth immediately, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a remote place﴾, and this indicates that there was a period between the conception and the birth in which she could withdraw with him.

Second: She carried him for nine hours and gave birth on the same day. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: Nine months. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Fourth: Three hours: she conceived him in one hour, he was formed in one hour, and she gave birth in one hour. This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

Fifth: Eight months, and he lived, and no child has ever lived born at eight months, so this was a sign. This was reported by al-Zajjaj.

Sixth: Six months. This was reported by al-Mawardi.

Seventh: In a single hour. This was reported by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she withdrew with him﴾, meaning with the pregnancy, ﴿to a remote place﴾, that is, a distant place. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿qasiyan﴾ as "qasiyan" (with the alif). Ibn Ishaq said: She walked six miles. al-Farra' said: al-qasiyy and al-qasi have the same meaning. Others than al-Farra' said: al-qasiyy and al-qasi are like al-shahid and al-shahid's counterpart (i.e., they are two forms of the same root with the same sense). She withdrew far only to flee from her people, lest they reproach her for bearing a child without a husband.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her﴾. ʿIkrimah, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read ﴿al-mikhad﴾ with a kasra on the mim. al-Farra' said: The meaning is: the labour pains brought her, and when the particle (bi, "with") was removed, an alif was placed in the verb, similar to ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾ [al-Kahf: 63], meaning "with our morning meal," and similar to ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], meaning "with blocks of iron." Abu 'Ubayda said: "ajā'ahā" is used of the one who came, and "ajā'a-hā" is used of someone else bringing her. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning is "he brought her and compelled her," from the expressions "need brought me to you" (jā'at bī al-ḥājatu ilayka) and "need compelled me to you" (ajā'atnī al-ḥājatu ilayka). al-Makhad means labour pains. Others said: al-makhad is the pain of childbirth.

﴿To the trunk of the palm tree﴾, which is the stem of the palm, and it was a dry palm standing in the desert, having neither a crown nor fronds.

﴿She said: "Oh, would that I had died before this"﴾, that is, before this day or this matter. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Hafs read ﴿mittu﴾ with a kasra on the mim.

There are two views on the reason for her saying this: One, she said it out of shame before people. The second, so that they would not sin by slandering her.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I had been a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿nasyan﴾ with a kasra on the nun. Hamzah and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿nasyan﴾ with a fatha on the nun. al-Farra' said: The companions of ʿAbd Allah read it with a fatha on the nun, while the rest of the Arabs read it with a kasra, and both are dialects, like al-jisr and al-jasr, and al-witr and al-wattr, and the fatha is more beloved to me. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: The kasra is according to both dialects. Ibn al-Anbari said: Whoever reads with a kasra says: al-nasy is a noun for what is forgotten, like al-bughd being a noun for what is hated, and al-sabb a noun for what is reviled. And al-nasy with a fatha is also a noun for what is forgotten, as a verbal noun that stands in place of the noun, as one says "al-rajul danif" and "danaf" (a sick man): the kasra form is the proper descriptive adjective, and the fatha form is a verbal noun that takes the place of the adjective. It is possible that al-nasy and al-nisy are two nouns with one meaning, as one says al-ritl and al-ratl (both meaning a pound).

The exegetes have five views regarding His saying: ﴿nasyan mansiyyan﴾: [p. 221]

First: "Would that I had not been anything." This was said by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿAta' and Ibn Zayd also said this.

Second: ﴿And I had been a thing forgotten﴾, that is, a discarded menstrual cloth. This was said by Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah. al-Farra' said: al-nasy is what a woman discards of her menstrual rags. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is the menstrual rags a woman throws away, which no one seeks or remembers.

Third: It is from miscarriage (al-saqt). This was said by Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Rabi'.

Fourth: The meaning is: "Would that I were unknown, and no one knew who I am." This was said by Qatada.

Fifth: It is a trivial thing that people leave behind on a journey, so it becomes insignificant to them and they do not return for it. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-nasy and al-mansiyy are what is forgotten of a water-skin or a staff, meaning that it is forgotten in the dwelling and no one returns for it, because its owner considers it worthless. al-Kisa'i said: The meaning of the verse is: "Would that I had been something which, when mentioned, would not be sought."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he called to her from below her﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a fatha on the mim and the ta'. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a kasra on the mim and the ta'. Whoever reads with a kasra on the mim has two interpretations: One: the angel called to her from beneath the palm tree. It was also said: she was on a raised ground, and the angel called to her from lower than her. The second: Jesus called to her when he came out of her womb. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Everything to which you raise your eye is above you, and everything to which you lower your eye is below you. Whoever reads with a fatha on the mim has the two interpretations mentioned. al-Farra' used to say: The one who addressed her was only the angel, according to both readings.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾. There are two views on this:

[p. 222] One: It is a small stream. This was said by the majority of exegetes and philologists. Abu Salih and Ibn Jurayj said: It is al-jadwal (a stream) in Syriac.

The second: It is Jesus, who was a "sariyy" (a noble, honoured one) among men. This was said by al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and [Ibn Zayd]. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Hasan retracted this view in favour of the first view. If it were a description of Jesus, he would be a "sariyy" youth or a "sawiyy" (a sound, upright one) among the boys, and the Arabs rarely say "I saw a noble with you" until they say "a noble man."

If it is asked: How does it fit her consolation that it was said: "Do not grieve, for here is a flowing stream"?

The answer has two aspects: One: She grieved over the barrenness of the place where she had given birth, the lack of food and drink, and the water with which to purify herself. So it was said: "Do not grieve, We have made a stream flow for you and caused fresh dates to fall for you." This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: She grieved over what had befallen her of bearing a child without a husband. So Allah, exalted is He, made a stream flow for her, which came to her from the Jordan, and brought forth dates for her from the dry tree, and that was a sign showing the power of Allah, exalted is He, in creating Jesus. This was said by Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And shake toward you﴾. Al-hazz means shaking.

The particle (bi, "with") in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the trunk of the palm tree﴾ has two views:

One: It is an additional, emphatic particle, like His saying: ﴿Let him extend a rope to the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]. al-Farra' said: The meaning is: "Let him extend a rope." The Arabs say: "hazzahu" and "hazza bihi" (both mean "he shook it"), and "khudh al-khitam" and "khudh bi-l-khitam" (both mean "take the halter"), and "ta'allaqa Zaydan" and "ta'allaqa bihi" (both mean "he clung to Zayd"). Abu ʿUbayda said: It is emphatic, like the saying of the poet:

*"We strike with the sword and hope for relief."*

[p. 223] The second: It entered the trunk to make it adhere to the shaking, so it is conveying attachment (ilsaq). This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿tusāqiṭ﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, al-Sakka'i and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ with a ta' and a doubled sin. Hamzah and ʿAbd al-Warith read ﴿tasāqaṭ﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a single sin. Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿tusāqiṭ﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the qaf, with a single sin. Ya'qub and Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal read ﴿yassāqaṭu﴾ with a fatha on the ya', a doubled sin, and a fatha on the qaf. These are the famous recitations. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu Haywa read ﴿taskutu﴾ with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the sin, and a damma on the qaf. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, ʿAisha and al-Hasan read ﴿yusāqiṭ﴾ with an alif, a single sin, a damma on the ya', and a kasra on the qaf. al-Dahhak and ʿAmr ibn Dinar read ﴿yusqiṭ﴾ with a damma on the ya', a kasra on the qaf, a sukun on the sin, and no alif. ʿAsim al-Jahdari and Abu ʿImran al-Jawni read the same, except with a ta'. Mu'adh al-Qari' and Ibn Ya'mur read the same, except with a nun. Abu Razin al-ʿUqaili and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿yasqut﴾ with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the sin, and a damma on the qaf. Abu al-Sammak al-ʿAdawi and Ibn Hizam read ﴿tatasāqaṭu﴾ with two fathas on the two ta's and an alif. al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads ﴿yassāqaṭ﴾, the meaning is ﴿yatasāqaṭ﴾, and the ta' was assimilated into the sin. Whoever reads ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ is the same, and used the feminine because the word "palm tree" (nakhla) is feminine. Whoever reads ﴿tasāqaṭ﴾ with a ta' and lightening, has removed from ﴿tatasāqaṭu﴾ the meeting of two ta's. Whoever reads ﴿yassāqaṭ﴾ intends the meaning: "the trunk fell down upon you." Whoever reads ﴿nusāqiṭ﴾ with a nun, the meaning is: "We shall cause it to fall upon you, and We make it a sign for you." The grammarians say: [p. 224] When you say ﴿yassāqaṭu﴾ or ﴿yatasāqaṭu﴾, ﴿ruṭaban﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The meaning is: "the trunk drops fresh dates." When you say ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ with a ta', the meaning is: "the palm tree drops fresh dates."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿janiyyan﴾. al-Farra' said: al-janiyy means "that which is picked." Ibn al-Anbari said: It is the fresh one, and the original form is "mujnū", which was changed from the pattern of maf'ul to fa'il, as one says "qadid" and "tabikh" (dried meat and cooked meat). Others said: It is the fresh one with its dust still on it. That palm tree had no crown, so Allah, exalted is He, caused it to grow, and when she placed her hand upon it, the fresh dates fell, fresh. The early generations (al-salaf) used to recommend fresh dates for women after childbirth, because of Maryam, peace be upon her.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat﴾, that is, of the fresh dates, ﴿and drink﴾ from the stream, ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ by the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him. al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "qarirat bihi ʿaynan, aqarru" (with the fatha on the qaf in the imperfect), and "qarrarat fi al-makan, aqarru" (with the kasra on the qaf); and "ʿaynan" is in the accusative as a specification. Ibn al-Anbari related from al-Asma'i that he said: The meaning of ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ is: "let your tears be cooled," because tears of joy are cool, and tears of grief are hot. The derivation of "qarri" is from al-qarur, which is cold water. Ahmad ibn Yahya said to us: The explanation of "qarri ʿaynan" is: you have reached the goal of your hope, so that your eye is cooled from looking toward anything else, and he cited the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*"On a day of dread, with striking and thrusting, by which your clients' eyes were made content."*

That is, they achieved victory and reached the end of their hopes, so their eyes were cooled from looking to anything else.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you see﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, al-Dahhak, Abu al-ʿAliya and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read ﴿tara'inna﴾ with a kasra on the hamza and no ya'. That is: if you see any human being, then say. There is an implied element in it, its estimated meaning being: "then if he asks you about the matter of your child." ﴿Then say: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast"﴾. There are two views on this: [p. 225]

One: silence (ṣamt). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas ibn Malik and al-Dahhak. Likewise Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Anas ibn Malik and Abu Razin al-ʿUqaili read ﴿ṣamtan﴾ in place of "ṣawman" (fast). Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿ṣiyaman﴾.

The second meaning: fasting from food, drink and speech. This is what Qatadah said. Ibn Zayd said: the diligent worshipper among the Children of Israel would fast from speech just as he fasts from food, except for the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As-Suddi said: so Allah permitted her to speak only this much, and then she would remain silent. Ibn Mas'ud said: she was commanded to silence, because she had no proof before the people, so she was commanded to refrain from speech so that her son would suffice her in speaking, by clearing her good name. It was also said: she would speak with the angels but would not speak with mankind. Ibn al-Anbari said: the word sawm (fasting, in the sense of abstention) in the language of the Arabs has four meanings. It is said: sawm for abstaining from food and drink; sawm for silence; sawm for a kind of tree; and sawm for the dung of the ostrich.

The scholars differed over the age of Maryam on the day she gave birth, giving three opinions:

The first: she gave birth when she was fifteen years old. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The second: she was twelve years old. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: she was thirteen years old. This was said by Muqatil.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 19, verses 22–26 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she conceived him﴾, meaning Jesus.

There are two views on how she conceived him:

One: Gabriel blew into the opening of her garment, and the conception continued in her. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Suddi said: He blew into the opening of her shift, which was slit at the front, and the breath entered her chest, and she conceived at that moment.

The second: The one who addressed her is the one who conceived him, and he entered through her mouth. This was said by Ubayy ibn Ka'b. [p. 219]

On the duration of her pregnancy there are seven views:

First: She gave birth as soon as she conceived. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and the meaning is that her pregnancy was not prolonged, not that she gave birth immediately, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a remote place﴾, and this indicates that there was a period between the conception and the birth in which she could withdraw with him.

Second: She carried him for nine hours and gave birth on the same day. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: Nine months. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Fourth: Three hours: she conceived him in one hour, he was formed in one hour, and she gave birth in one hour. This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

Fifth: Eight months, and he lived, and no child has ever lived born at eight months, so this was a sign. This was reported by al-Zajjaj.

Sixth: Six months. This was reported by al-Mawardi.

Seventh: In a single hour. This was reported by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she withdrew with him﴾, meaning with the pregnancy, ﴿to a remote place﴾, that is, a distant place. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿qasiyan﴾ as "qasiyan" (with the alif). Ibn Ishaq said: She walked six miles. al-Farra' said: al-qasiyy and al-qasi have the same meaning. Others than al-Farra' said: al-qasiyy and al-qasi are like al-shahid and al-shahid's counterpart (i.e., they are two forms of the same root with the same sense). She withdrew far only to flee from her people, lest they reproach her for bearing a child without a husband.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her﴾. ʿIkrimah, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read ﴿al-mikhad﴾ with a kasra on the mim. al-Farra' said: The meaning is: the labour pains brought her, and when the particle (bi, "with") was removed, an alif was placed in the verb, similar to ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾ [al-Kahf: 63], meaning "with our morning meal," and similar to ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], meaning "with blocks of iron." Abu 'Ubayda said: "ajā'ahā" is used of the one who came, and "ajā'a-hā" is used of someone else bringing her. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning is "he brought her and compelled her," from the expressions "need brought me to you" (jā'at bī al-ḥājatu ilayka) and "need compelled me to you" (ajā'atnī al-ḥājatu ilayka). al-Makhad means labour pains. Others said: al-makhad is the pain of childbirth.

﴿To the trunk of the palm tree﴾, which is the stem of the palm, and it was a dry palm standing in the desert, having neither a crown nor fronds.

﴿She said: "Oh, would that I had died before this"﴾, that is, before this day or this matter. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Hafs read ﴿mittu﴾ with a kasra on the mim.

There are two views on the reason for her saying this: One, she said it out of shame before people. The second, so that they would not sin by slandering her.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I had been a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿nasyan﴾ with a kasra on the nun. Hamzah and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿nasyan﴾ with a fatha on the nun. al-Farra' said: The companions of ʿAbd Allah read it with a fatha on the nun, while the rest of the Arabs read it with a kasra, and both are dialects, like al-jisr and al-jasr, and al-witr and al-wattr, and the fatha is more beloved to me. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: The kasra is according to both dialects. Ibn al-Anbari said: Whoever reads with a kasra says: al-nasy is a noun for what is forgotten, like al-bughd being a noun for what is hated, and al-sabb a noun for what is reviled. And al-nasy with a fatha is also a noun for what is forgotten, as a verbal noun that stands in place of the noun, as one says "al-rajul danif" and "danaf" (a sick man): the kasra form is the proper descriptive adjective, and the fatha form is a verbal noun that takes the place of the adjective. It is possible that al-nasy and al-nisy are two nouns with one meaning, as one says al-ritl and al-ratl (both meaning a pound).

The exegetes have five views regarding His saying: ﴿nasyan mansiyyan﴾: [p. 221]

First: "Would that I had not been anything." This was said by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿAta' and Ibn Zayd also said this.

Second: ﴿And I had been a thing forgotten﴾, that is, a discarded menstrual cloth. This was said by Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah. al-Farra' said: al-nasy is what a woman discards of her menstrual rags. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is the menstrual rags a woman throws away, which no one seeks or remembers.

Third: It is from miscarriage (al-saqt). This was said by Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Rabi'.

Fourth: The meaning is: "Would that I were unknown, and no one knew who I am." This was said by Qatada.

Fifth: It is a trivial thing that people leave behind on a journey, so it becomes insignificant to them and they do not return for it. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-nasy and al-mansiyy are what is forgotten of a water-skin or a staff, meaning that it is forgotten in the dwelling and no one returns for it, because its owner considers it worthless. al-Kisa'i said: The meaning of the verse is: "Would that I had been something which, when mentioned, would not be sought."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he called to her from below her﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a fatha on the mim and the ta'. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a kasra on the mim and the ta'. Whoever reads with a kasra on the mim has two interpretations: One: the angel called to her from beneath the palm tree. It was also said: she was on a raised ground, and the angel called to her from lower than her. The second: Jesus called to her when he came out of her womb. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Everything to which you raise your eye is above you, and everything to which you lower your eye is below you. Whoever reads with a fatha on the mim has the two interpretations mentioned. al-Farra' used to say: The one who addressed her was only the angel, according to both readings.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾. There are two views on this:

[p. 222] One: It is a small stream. This was said by the majority of exegetes and philologists. Abu Salih and Ibn Jurayj said: It is al-jadwal (a stream) in Syriac.

The second: It is Jesus, who was a "sariyy" (a noble, honoured one) among men. This was said by al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and [Ibn Zayd]. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Hasan retracted this view in favour of the first view. If it were a description of Jesus, he would be a "sariyy" youth or a "sawiyy" (a sound, upright one) among the boys, and the Arabs rarely say "I saw a noble with you" until they say "a noble man."

If it is asked: How does it fit her consolation that it was said: "Do not grieve, for here is a flowing stream"?

The answer has two aspects: One: She grieved over the barrenness of the place where she had given birth, the lack of food and drink, and the water with which to purify herself. So it was said: "Do not grieve, We have made a stream flow for you and caused fresh dates to fall for you." This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: She grieved over what had befallen her of bearing a child without a husband. So Allah, exalted is He, made a stream flow for her, which came to her from the Jordan, and brought forth dates for her from the dry tree, and that was a sign showing the power of Allah, exalted is He, in creating Jesus. This was said by Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And shake toward you﴾. Al-hazz means shaking.

The particle (bi, "with") in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the trunk of the palm tree﴾ has two views:

One: It is an additional, emphatic particle, like His saying: ﴿Let him extend a rope to the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]. al-Farra' said: The meaning is: "Let him extend a rope." The Arabs say: "hazzahu" and "hazza bihi" (both mean "he shook it"), and "khudh al-khitam" and "khudh bi-l-khitam" (both mean "take the halter"), and "ta'allaqa Zaydan" and "ta'allaqa bihi" (both mean "he clung to Zayd"). Abu ʿUbayda said: It is emphatic, like the saying of the poet:

*"We strike with the sword and hope for relief."*

[p. 223] The second: It entered the trunk to make it adhere to the shaking, so it is conveying attachment (ilsaq). This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿tusāqiṭ﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, al-Sakka'i and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ with a ta' and a doubled sin. Hamzah and ʿAbd al-Warith read ﴿tasāqaṭ﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a single sin. Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿tusāqiṭ﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the qaf, with a single sin. Ya'qub and Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal read ﴿yassāqaṭu﴾ with a fatha on the ya', a doubled sin, and a fatha on the qaf. These are the famous recitations. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu Haywa read ﴿taskutu﴾ with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the sin, and a damma on the qaf. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, ʿAisha and al-Hasan read ﴿yusāqiṭ﴾ with an alif, a single sin, a damma on the ya', and a kasra on the qaf. al-Dahhak and ʿAmr ibn Dinar read ﴿yusqiṭ﴾ with a damma on the ya', a kasra on the qaf, a sukun on the sin, and no alif. ʿAsim al-Jahdari and Abu ʿImran al-Jawni read the same, except with a ta'. Mu'adh al-Qari' and Ibn Ya'mur read the same, except with a nun. Abu Razin al-ʿUqaili and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿yasqut﴾ with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the sin, and a damma on the qaf. Abu al-Sammak al-ʿAdawi and Ibn Hizam read ﴿tatasāqaṭu﴾ with two fathas on the two ta's and an alif. al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads ﴿yassāqaṭ﴾, the meaning is ﴿yatasāqaṭ﴾, and the ta' was assimilated into the sin. Whoever reads ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ is the same, and used the feminine because the word "palm tree" (nakhla) is feminine. Whoever reads ﴿tasāqaṭ﴾ with a ta' and lightening, has removed from ﴿tatasāqaṭu﴾ the meeting of two ta's. Whoever reads ﴿yassāqaṭ﴾ intends the meaning: "the trunk fell down upon you." Whoever reads ﴿nusāqiṭ﴾ with a nun, the meaning is: "We shall cause it to fall upon you, and We make it a sign for you." The grammarians say: [p. 224] When you say ﴿yassāqaṭu﴾ or ﴿yatasāqaṭu﴾, ﴿ruṭaban﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The meaning is: "the trunk drops fresh dates." When you say ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ with a ta', the meaning is: "the palm tree drops fresh dates."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿janiyyan﴾. al-Farra' said: al-janiyy means "that which is picked." Ibn al-Anbari said: It is the fresh one, and the original form is "mujnū", which was changed from the pattern of maf'ul to fa'il, as one says "qadid" and "tabikh" (dried meat and cooked meat). Others said: It is the fresh one with its dust still on it. That palm tree had no crown, so Allah, exalted is He, caused it to grow, and when she placed her hand upon it, the fresh dates fell, fresh. The early generations (al-salaf) used to recommend fresh dates for women after childbirth, because of Maryam, peace be upon her.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat﴾, that is, of the fresh dates, ﴿and drink﴾ from the stream, ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ by the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him. al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "qarirat bihi ʿaynan, aqarru" (with the fatha on the qaf in the imperfect), and "qarrarat fi al-makan, aqarru" (with the kasra on the qaf); and "ʿaynan" is in the accusative as a specification. Ibn al-Anbari related from al-Asma'i that he said: The meaning of ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ is: "let your tears be cooled," because tears of joy are cool, and tears of grief are hot. The derivation of "qarri" is from al-qarur, which is cold water. Ahmad ibn Yahya said to us: The explanation of "qarri ʿaynan" is: you have reached the goal of your hope, so that your eye is cooled from looking toward anything else, and he cited the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*"On a day of dread, with striking and thrusting, by which your clients' eyes were made content."*

That is, they achieved victory and reached the end of their hopes, so their eyes were cooled from looking to anything else.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you see﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, al-Dahhak, Abu al-ʿAliya and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read ﴿tara'inna﴾ with a kasra on the hamza and no ya'. That is: if you see any human being, then say. There is an implied element in it, its estimated meaning being: "then if he asks you about the matter of your child." ﴿Then say: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast"﴾. There are two views on this: [p. 225]

One: silence (ṣamt). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas ibn Malik and al-Dahhak. Likewise Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Anas ibn Malik and Abu Razin al-ʿUqaili read ﴿ṣamtan﴾ in place of "ṣawman" (fast). Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿ṣiyaman﴾.

The second meaning: fasting from food, drink and speech. This is what Qatadah said. Ibn Zayd said: the diligent worshipper among the Children of Israel would fast from speech just as he fasts from food, except for the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As-Suddi said: so Allah permitted her to speak only this much, and then she would remain silent. Ibn Mas'ud said: she was commanded to silence, because she had no proof before the people, so she was commanded to refrain from speech so that her son would suffice her in speaking, by clearing her good name. It was also said: she would speak with the angels but would not speak with mankind. Ibn al-Anbari said: the word sawm (fasting, in the sense of abstention) in the language of the Arabs has four meanings. It is said: sawm for abstaining from food and drink; sawm for silence; sawm for a kind of tree; and sawm for the dung of the ostrich.

The scholars differed over the age of Maryam on the day she gave birth, giving three opinions:

The first: she gave birth when she was fifteen years old. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The second: she was twelve years old. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: she was thirteen years old. This was said by Muqatil.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 19, verses 22–26 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she conceived him﴾, meaning Jesus.

There are two views on how she conceived him:

One: Gabriel blew into the opening of her garment, and the conception continued in her. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Suddi said: He blew into the opening of her shift, which was slit at the front, and the breath entered her chest, and she conceived at that moment.

The second: The one who addressed her is the one who conceived him, and he entered through her mouth. This was said by Ubayy ibn Ka'b. [p. 219]

On the duration of her pregnancy there are seven views:

First: She gave birth as soon as she conceived. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and the meaning is that her pregnancy was not prolonged, not that she gave birth immediately, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a remote place﴾, and this indicates that there was a period between the conception and the birth in which she could withdraw with him.

Second: She carried him for nine hours and gave birth on the same day. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: Nine months. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Fourth: Three hours: she conceived him in one hour, he was formed in one hour, and she gave birth in one hour. This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

Fifth: Eight months, and he lived, and no child has ever lived born at eight months, so this was a sign. This was reported by al-Zajjaj.

Sixth: Six months. This was reported by al-Mawardi.

Seventh: In a single hour. This was reported by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she withdrew with him﴾, meaning with the pregnancy, ﴿to a remote place﴾, that is, a distant place. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿qasiyan﴾ as "qasiyan" (with the alif). Ibn Ishaq said: She walked six miles. al-Farra' said: al-qasiyy and al-qasi have the same meaning. Others than al-Farra' said: al-qasiyy and al-qasi are like al-shahid and al-shahid's counterpart (i.e., they are two forms of the same root with the same sense). She withdrew far only to flee from her people, lest they reproach her for bearing a child without a husband.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her﴾. ʿIkrimah, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read ﴿al-mikhad﴾ with a kasra on the mim. al-Farra' said: The meaning is: the labour pains brought her, and when the particle (bi, "with") was removed, an alif was placed in the verb, similar to ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾ [al-Kahf: 63], meaning "with our morning meal," and similar to ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], meaning "with blocks of iron." Abu 'Ubayda said: "ajā'ahā" is used of the one who came, and "ajā'a-hā" is used of someone else bringing her. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning is "he brought her and compelled her," from the expressions "need brought me to you" (jā'at bī al-ḥājatu ilayka) and "need compelled me to you" (ajā'atnī al-ḥājatu ilayka). al-Makhad means labour pains. Others said: al-makhad is the pain of childbirth.

﴿To the trunk of the palm tree﴾, which is the stem of the palm, and it was a dry palm standing in the desert, having neither a crown nor fronds.

﴿She said: "Oh, would that I had died before this"﴾, that is, before this day or this matter. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Hafs read ﴿mittu﴾ with a kasra on the mim.

There are two views on the reason for her saying this: One, she said it out of shame before people. The second, so that they would not sin by slandering her.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I had been a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿nasyan﴾ with a kasra on the nun. Hamzah and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿nasyan﴾ with a fatha on the nun. al-Farra' said: The companions of ʿAbd Allah read it with a fatha on the nun, while the rest of the Arabs read it with a kasra, and both are dialects, like al-jisr and al-jasr, and al-witr and al-wattr, and the fatha is more beloved to me. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: The kasra is according to both dialects. Ibn al-Anbari said: Whoever reads with a kasra says: al-nasy is a noun for what is forgotten, like al-bughd being a noun for what is hated, and al-sabb a noun for what is reviled. And al-nasy with a fatha is also a noun for what is forgotten, as a verbal noun that stands in place of the noun, as one says "al-rajul danif" and "danaf" (a sick man): the kasra form is the proper descriptive adjective, and the fatha form is a verbal noun that takes the place of the adjective. It is possible that al-nasy and al-nisy are two nouns with one meaning, as one says al-ritl and al-ratl (both meaning a pound).

The exegetes have five views regarding His saying: ﴿nasyan mansiyyan﴾: [p. 221]

First: "Would that I had not been anything." This was said by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿAta' and Ibn Zayd also said this.

Second: ﴿And I had been a thing forgotten﴾, that is, a discarded menstrual cloth. This was said by Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah. al-Farra' said: al-nasy is what a woman discards of her menstrual rags. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is the menstrual rags a woman throws away, which no one seeks or remembers.

Third: It is from miscarriage (al-saqt). This was said by Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Rabi'.

Fourth: The meaning is: "Would that I were unknown, and no one knew who I am." This was said by Qatada.

Fifth: It is a trivial thing that people leave behind on a journey, so it becomes insignificant to them and they do not return for it. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-nasy and al-mansiyy are what is forgotten of a water-skin or a staff, meaning that it is forgotten in the dwelling and no one returns for it, because its owner considers it worthless. al-Kisa'i said: The meaning of the verse is: "Would that I had been something which, when mentioned, would not be sought."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he called to her from below her﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a fatha on the mim and the ta'. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a kasra on the mim and the ta'. Whoever reads with a kasra on the mim has two interpretations: One: the angel called to her from beneath the palm tree. It was also said: she was on a raised ground, and the angel called to her from lower than her. The second: Jesus called to her when he came out of her womb. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Everything to which you raise your eye is above you, and everything to which you lower your eye is below you. Whoever reads with a fatha on the mim has the two interpretations mentioned. al-Farra' used to say: The one who addressed her was only the angel, according to both readings.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾. There are two views on this:

[p. 222] One: It is a small stream. This was said by the majority of exegetes and philologists. Abu Salih and Ibn Jurayj said: It is al-jadwal (a stream) in Syriac.

The second: It is Jesus, who was a "sariyy" (a noble, honoured one) among men. This was said by al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and [Ibn Zayd]. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Hasan retracted this view in favour of the first view. If it were a description of Jesus, he would be a "sariyy" youth or a "sawiyy" (a sound, upright one) among the boys, and the Arabs rarely say "I saw a noble with you" until they say "a noble man."

If it is asked: How does it fit her consolation that it was said: "Do not grieve, for here is a flowing stream"?

The answer has two aspects: One: She grieved over the barrenness of the place where she had given birth, the lack of food and drink, and the water with which to purify herself. So it was said: "Do not grieve, We have made a stream flow for you and caused fresh dates to fall for you." This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: She grieved over what had befallen her of bearing a child without a husband. So Allah, exalted is He, made a stream flow for her, which came to her from the Jordan, and brought forth dates for her from the dry tree, and that was a sign showing the power of Allah, exalted is He, in creating Jesus. This was said by Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And shake toward you﴾. Al-hazz means shaking.

The particle (bi, "with") in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the trunk of the palm tree﴾ has two views:

One: It is an additional, emphatic particle, like His saying: ﴿Let him extend a rope to the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]. al-Farra' said: The meaning is: "Let him extend a rope." The Arabs say: "hazzahu" and "hazza bihi" (both mean "he shook it"), and "khudh al-khitam" and "khudh bi-l-khitam" (both mean "take the halter"), and "ta'allaqa Zaydan" and "ta'allaqa bihi" (both mean "he clung to Zayd"). Abu ʿUbayda said: It is emphatic, like the saying of the poet:

*"We strike with the sword and hope for relief."*

[p. 223] The second: It entered the trunk to make it adhere to the shaking, so it is conveying attachment (ilsaq). This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿tusāqiṭ﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, al-Sakka'i and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ with a ta' and a doubled sin. Hamzah and ʿAbd al-Warith read ﴿tasāqaṭ﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a single sin. Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿tusāqiṭ﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the qaf, with a single sin. Ya'qub and Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal read ﴿yassāqaṭu﴾ with a fatha on the ya', a doubled sin, and a fatha on the qaf. These are the famous recitations. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu Haywa read ﴿taskutu﴾ with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the sin, and a damma on the qaf. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, ʿAisha and al-Hasan read ﴿yusāqiṭ﴾ with an alif, a single sin, a damma on the ya', and a kasra on the qaf. al-Dahhak and ʿAmr ibn Dinar read ﴿yusqiṭ﴾ with a damma on the ya', a kasra on the qaf, a sukun on the sin, and no alif. ʿAsim al-Jahdari and Abu ʿImran al-Jawni read the same, except with a ta'. Mu'adh al-Qari' and Ibn Ya'mur read the same, except with a nun. Abu Razin al-ʿUqaili and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿yasqut﴾ with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the sin, and a damma on the qaf. Abu al-Sammak al-ʿAdawi and Ibn Hizam read ﴿tatasāqaṭu﴾ with two fathas on the two ta's and an alif. al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads ﴿yassāqaṭ﴾, the meaning is ﴿yatasāqaṭ﴾, and the ta' was assimilated into the sin. Whoever reads ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ is the same, and used the feminine because the word "palm tree" (nakhla) is feminine. Whoever reads ﴿tasāqaṭ﴾ with a ta' and lightening, has removed from ﴿tatasāqaṭu﴾ the meeting of two ta's. Whoever reads ﴿yassāqaṭ﴾ intends the meaning: "the trunk fell down upon you." Whoever reads ﴿nusāqiṭ﴾ with a nun, the meaning is: "We shall cause it to fall upon you, and We make it a sign for you." The grammarians say: [p. 224] When you say ﴿yassāqaṭu﴾ or ﴿yatasāqaṭu﴾, ﴿ruṭaban﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The meaning is: "the trunk drops fresh dates." When you say ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ with a ta', the meaning is: "the palm tree drops fresh dates."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿janiyyan﴾. al-Farra' said: al-janiyy means "that which is picked." Ibn al-Anbari said: It is the fresh one, and the original form is "mujnū", which was changed from the pattern of maf'ul to fa'il, as one says "qadid" and "tabikh" (dried meat and cooked meat). Others said: It is the fresh one with its dust still on it. That palm tree had no crown, so Allah, exalted is He, caused it to grow, and when she placed her hand upon it, the fresh dates fell, fresh. The early generations (al-salaf) used to recommend fresh dates for women after childbirth, because of Maryam, peace be upon her.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat﴾, that is, of the fresh dates, ﴿and drink﴾ from the stream, ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ by the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him. al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "qarirat bihi ʿaynan, aqarru" (with the fatha on the qaf in the imperfect), and "qarrarat fi al-makan, aqarru" (with the kasra on the qaf); and "ʿaynan" is in the accusative as a specification. Ibn al-Anbari related from al-Asma'i that he said: The meaning of ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ is: "let your tears be cooled," because tears of joy are cool, and tears of grief are hot. The derivation of "qarri" is from al-qarur, which is cold water. Ahmad ibn Yahya said to us: The explanation of "qarri ʿaynan" is: you have reached the goal of your hope, so that your eye is cooled from looking toward anything else, and he cited the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*"On a day of dread, with striking and thrusting, by which your clients' eyes were made content."*

That is, they achieved victory and reached the end of their hopes, so their eyes were cooled from looking to anything else.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you see﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, al-Dahhak, Abu al-ʿAliya and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read ﴿tara'inna﴾ with a kasra on the hamza and no ya'. That is: if you see any human being, then say. There is an implied element in it, its estimated meaning being: "then if he asks you about the matter of your child." ﴿Then say: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast"﴾. There are two views on this: [p. 225]

One: silence (ṣamt). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas ibn Malik and al-Dahhak. Likewise Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Anas ibn Malik and Abu Razin al-ʿUqaili read ﴿ṣamtan﴾ in place of "ṣawman" (fast). Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿ṣiyaman﴾.

The second meaning: fasting from food, drink and speech. This is what Qatadah said. Ibn Zayd said: the diligent worshipper among the Children of Israel would fast from speech just as he fasts from food, except for the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As-Suddi said: so Allah permitted her to speak only this much, and then she would remain silent. Ibn Mas'ud said: she was commanded to silence, because she had no proof before the people, so she was commanded to refrain from speech so that her son would suffice her in speaking, by clearing her good name. It was also said: she would speak with the angels but would not speak with mankind. Ibn al-Anbari said: the word sawm (fasting, in the sense of abstention) in the language of the Arabs has four meanings. It is said: sawm for abstaining from food and drink; sawm for silence; sawm for a kind of tree; and sawm for the dung of the ostrich.

The scholars differed over the age of Maryam on the day she gave birth, giving three opinions:

The first: she gave birth when she was fifteen years old. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The second: she was twelve years old. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: she was thirteen years old. This was said by Muqatil.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 19, verses 22–26 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she conceived him﴾, meaning Jesus.

There are two views on how she conceived him:

One: Gabriel blew into the opening of her garment, and the conception continued in her. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Suddi said: He blew into the opening of her shift, which was slit at the front, and the breath entered her chest, and she conceived at that moment.

The second: The one who addressed her is the one who conceived him, and he entered through her mouth. This was said by Ubayy ibn Ka'b. [p. 219]

On the duration of her pregnancy there are seven views:

First: She gave birth as soon as she conceived. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and the meaning is that her pregnancy was not prolonged, not that she gave birth immediately, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a remote place﴾, and this indicates that there was a period between the conception and the birth in which she could withdraw with him.

Second: She carried him for nine hours and gave birth on the same day. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: Nine months. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Fourth: Three hours: she conceived him in one hour, he was formed in one hour, and she gave birth in one hour. This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

Fifth: Eight months, and he lived, and no child has ever lived born at eight months, so this was a sign. This was reported by al-Zajjaj.

Sixth: Six months. This was reported by al-Mawardi.

Seventh: In a single hour. This was reported by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she withdrew with him﴾, meaning with the pregnancy, ﴿to a remote place﴾, that is, a distant place. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿qasiyan﴾ as "qasiyan" (with the alif). Ibn Ishaq said: She walked six miles. al-Farra' said: al-qasiyy and al-qasi have the same meaning. Others than al-Farra' said: al-qasiyy and al-qasi are like al-shahid and al-shahid's counterpart (i.e., they are two forms of the same root with the same sense). She withdrew far only to flee from her people, lest they reproach her for bearing a child without a husband.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her﴾. ʿIkrimah, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read ﴿al-mikhad﴾ with a kasra on the mim. al-Farra' said: The meaning is: the labour pains brought her, and when the particle (bi, "with") was removed, an alif was placed in the verb, similar to ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾ [al-Kahf: 63], meaning "with our morning meal," and similar to ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], meaning "with blocks of iron." Abu 'Ubayda said: "ajā'ahā" is used of the one who came, and "ajā'a-hā" is used of someone else bringing her. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning is "he brought her and compelled her," from the expressions "need brought me to you" (jā'at bī al-ḥājatu ilayka) and "need compelled me to you" (ajā'atnī al-ḥājatu ilayka). al-Makhad means labour pains. Others said: al-makhad is the pain of childbirth.

﴿To the trunk of the palm tree﴾, which is the stem of the palm, and it was a dry palm standing in the desert, having neither a crown nor fronds.

﴿She said: "Oh, would that I had died before this"﴾, that is, before this day or this matter. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Hafs read ﴿mittu﴾ with a kasra on the mim.

There are two views on the reason for her saying this: One, she said it out of shame before people. The second, so that they would not sin by slandering her.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I had been a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿nasyan﴾ with a kasra on the nun. Hamzah and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿nasyan﴾ with a fatha on the nun. al-Farra' said: The companions of ʿAbd Allah read it with a fatha on the nun, while the rest of the Arabs read it with a kasra, and both are dialects, like al-jisr and al-jasr, and al-witr and al-wattr, and the fatha is more beloved to me. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: The kasra is according to both dialects. Ibn al-Anbari said: Whoever reads with a kasra says: al-nasy is a noun for what is forgotten, like al-bughd being a noun for what is hated, and al-sabb a noun for what is reviled. And al-nasy with a fatha is also a noun for what is forgotten, as a verbal noun that stands in place of the noun, as one says "al-rajul danif" and "danaf" (a sick man): the kasra form is the proper descriptive adjective, and the fatha form is a verbal noun that takes the place of the adjective. It is possible that al-nasy and al-nisy are two nouns with one meaning, as one says al-ritl and al-ratl (both meaning a pound).

The exegetes have five views regarding His saying: ﴿nasyan mansiyyan﴾: [p. 221]

First: "Would that I had not been anything." This was said by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿAta' and Ibn Zayd also said this.

Second: ﴿And I had been a thing forgotten﴾, that is, a discarded menstrual cloth. This was said by Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah. al-Farra' said: al-nasy is what a woman discards of her menstrual rags. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is the menstrual rags a woman throws away, which no one seeks or remembers.

Third: It is from miscarriage (al-saqt). This was said by Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Rabi'.

Fourth: The meaning is: "Would that I were unknown, and no one knew who I am." This was said by Qatada.

Fifth: It is a trivial thing that people leave behind on a journey, so it becomes insignificant to them and they do not return for it. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-nasy and al-mansiyy are what is forgotten of a water-skin or a staff, meaning that it is forgotten in the dwelling and no one returns for it, because its owner considers it worthless. al-Kisa'i said: The meaning of the verse is: "Would that I had been something which, when mentioned, would not be sought."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he called to her from below her﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a fatha on the mim and the ta'. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a kasra on the mim and the ta'. Whoever reads with a kasra on the mim has two interpretations: One: the angel called to her from beneath the palm tree. It was also said: she was on a raised ground, and the angel called to her from lower than her. The second: Jesus called to her when he came out of her womb. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Everything to which you raise your eye is above you, and everything to which you lower your eye is below you. Whoever reads with a fatha on the mim has the two interpretations mentioned. al-Farra' used to say: The one who addressed her was only the angel, according to both readings.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾. There are two views on this:

[p. 222] One: It is a small stream. This was said by the majority of exegetes and philologists. Abu Salih and Ibn Jurayj said: It is al-jadwal (a stream) in Syriac.

The second: It is Jesus, who was a "sariyy" (a noble, honoured one) among men. This was said by al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and [Ibn Zayd]. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Hasan retracted this view in favour of the first view. If it were a description of Jesus, he would be a "sariyy" youth or a "sawiyy" (a sound, upright one) among the boys, and the Arabs rarely say "I saw a noble with you" until they say "a noble man."

If it is asked: How does it fit her consolation that it was said: "Do not grieve, for here is a flowing stream"?

The answer has two aspects: One: She grieved over the barrenness of the place where she had given birth, the lack of food and drink, and the water with which to purify herself. So it was said: "Do not grieve, We have made a stream flow for you and caused fresh dates to fall for you." This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: She grieved over what had befallen her of bearing a child without a husband. So Allah, exalted is He, made a stream flow for her, which came to her from the Jordan, and brought forth dates for her from the dry tree, and that was a sign showing the power of Allah, exalted is He, in creating Jesus. This was said by Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And shake toward you﴾. Al-hazz means shaking.

The particle (bi, "with") in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the trunk of the palm tree﴾ has two views:

One: It is an additional, emphatic particle, like His saying: ﴿Let him extend a rope to the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]. al-Farra' said: The meaning is: "Let him extend a rope." The Arabs say: "hazzahu" and "hazza bihi" (both mean "he shook it"), and "khudh al-khitam" and "khudh bi-l-khitam" (both mean "take the halter"), and "ta'allaqa Zaydan" and "ta'allaqa bihi" (both mean "he clung to Zayd"). Abu ʿUbayda said: It is emphatic, like the saying of the poet:

*"We strike with the sword and hope for relief."*

[p. 223] The second: It entered the trunk to make it adhere to the shaking, so it is conveying attachment (ilsaq). This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿tusāqiṭ﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, al-Sakka'i and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ with a ta' and a doubled sin. Hamzah and ʿAbd al-Warith read ﴿tasāqaṭ﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a single sin. Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿tusāqiṭ﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the qaf, with a single sin. Ya'qub and Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal read ﴿yassāqaṭu﴾ with a fatha on the ya', a doubled sin, and a fatha on the qaf. These are the famous recitations. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu Haywa read ﴿taskutu﴾ with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the sin, and a damma on the qaf. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, ʿAisha and al-Hasan read ﴿yusāqiṭ﴾ with an alif, a single sin, a damma on the ya', and a kasra on the qaf. al-Dahhak and ʿAmr ibn Dinar read ﴿yusqiṭ﴾ with a damma on the ya', a kasra on the qaf, a sukun on the sin, and no alif. ʿAsim al-Jahdari and Abu ʿImran al-Jawni read the same, except with a ta'. Mu'adh al-Qari' and Ibn Ya'mur read the same, except with a nun. Abu Razin al-ʿUqaili and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿yasqut﴾ with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the sin, and a damma on the qaf. Abu al-Sammak al-ʿAdawi and Ibn Hizam read ﴿tatasāqaṭu﴾ with two fathas on the two ta's and an alif. al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads ﴿yassāqaṭ﴾, the meaning is ﴿yatasāqaṭ﴾, and the ta' was assimilated into the sin. Whoever reads ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ is the same, and used the feminine because the word "palm tree" (nakhla) is feminine. Whoever reads ﴿tasāqaṭ﴾ with a ta' and lightening, has removed from ﴿tatasāqaṭu﴾ the meeting of two ta's. Whoever reads ﴿yassāqaṭ﴾ intends the meaning: "the trunk fell down upon you." Whoever reads ﴿nusāqiṭ﴾ with a nun, the meaning is: "We shall cause it to fall upon you, and We make it a sign for you." The grammarians say: [p. 224] When you say ﴿yassāqaṭu﴾ or ﴿yatasāqaṭu﴾, ﴿ruṭaban﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The meaning is: "the trunk drops fresh dates." When you say ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ with a ta', the meaning is: "the palm tree drops fresh dates."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿janiyyan﴾. al-Farra' said: al-janiyy means "that which is picked." Ibn al-Anbari said: It is the fresh one, and the original form is "mujnū", which was changed from the pattern of maf'ul to fa'il, as one says "qadid" and "tabikh" (dried meat and cooked meat). Others said: It is the fresh one with its dust still on it. That palm tree had no crown, so Allah, exalted is He, caused it to grow, and when she placed her hand upon it, the fresh dates fell, fresh. The early generations (al-salaf) used to recommend fresh dates for women after childbirth, because of Maryam, peace be upon her.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat﴾, that is, of the fresh dates, ﴿and drink﴾ from the stream, ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ by the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him. al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "qarirat bihi ʿaynan, aqarru" (with the fatha on the qaf in the imperfect), and "qarrarat fi al-makan, aqarru" (with the kasra on the qaf); and "ʿaynan" is in the accusative as a specification. Ibn al-Anbari related from al-Asma'i that he said: The meaning of ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ is: "let your tears be cooled," because tears of joy are cool, and tears of grief are hot. The derivation of "qarri" is from al-qarur, which is cold water. Ahmad ibn Yahya said to us: The explanation of "qarri ʿaynan" is: you have reached the goal of your hope, so that your eye is cooled from looking toward anything else, and he cited the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*"On a day of dread, with striking and thrusting, by which your clients' eyes were made content."*

That is, they achieved victory and reached the end of their hopes, so their eyes were cooled from looking to anything else.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you see﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, al-Dahhak, Abu al-ʿAliya and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read ﴿tara'inna﴾ with a kasra on the hamza and no ya'. That is: if you see any human being, then say. There is an implied element in it, its estimated meaning being: "then if he asks you about the matter of your child." ﴿Then say: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast"﴾. There are two views on this: [p. 225]

One: silence (ṣamt). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas ibn Malik and al-Dahhak. Likewise Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Anas ibn Malik and Abu Razin al-ʿUqaili read ﴿ṣamtan﴾ in place of "ṣawman" (fast). Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿ṣiyaman﴾.

The second meaning: fasting from food, drink and speech. This is what Qatadah said. Ibn Zayd said: the diligent worshipper among the Children of Israel would fast from speech just as he fasts from food, except for the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As-Suddi said: so Allah permitted her to speak only this much, and then she would remain silent. Ibn Mas'ud said: she was commanded to silence, because she had no proof before the people, so she was commanded to refrain from speech so that her son would suffice her in speaking, by clearing her good name. It was also said: she would speak with the angels but would not speak with mankind. Ibn al-Anbari said: the word sawm (fasting, in the sense of abstention) in the language of the Arabs has four meanings. It is said: sawm for abstaining from food and drink; sawm for silence; sawm for a kind of tree; and sawm for the dung of the ostrich.

The scholars differed over the age of Maryam on the day she gave birth, giving three opinions:

The first: she gave birth when she was fifteen years old. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The second: she was twelve years old. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: she was thirteen years old. This was said by Muqatil.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 19, verses 22–26 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she conceived him﴾, meaning Jesus.

There are two views on how she conceived him:

One: Gabriel blew into the opening of her garment, and the conception continued in her. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Suddi said: He blew into the opening of her shift, which was slit at the front, and the breath entered her chest, and she conceived at that moment.

The second: The one who addressed her is the one who conceived him, and he entered through her mouth. This was said by Ubayy ibn Ka'b. [p. 219]

On the duration of her pregnancy there are seven views:

First: She gave birth as soon as she conceived. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and the meaning is that her pregnancy was not prolonged, not that she gave birth immediately, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a remote place﴾, and this indicates that there was a period between the conception and the birth in which she could withdraw with him.

Second: She carried him for nine hours and gave birth on the same day. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: Nine months. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Fourth: Three hours: she conceived him in one hour, he was formed in one hour, and she gave birth in one hour. This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

Fifth: Eight months, and he lived, and no child has ever lived born at eight months, so this was a sign. This was reported by al-Zajjaj.

Sixth: Six months. This was reported by al-Mawardi.

Seventh: In a single hour. This was reported by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she withdrew with him﴾, meaning with the pregnancy, ﴿to a remote place﴾, that is, a distant place. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿qasiyan﴾ as "qasiyan" (with the alif). Ibn Ishaq said: She walked six miles. al-Farra' said: al-qasiyy and al-qasi have the same meaning. Others than al-Farra' said: al-qasiyy and al-qasi are like al-shahid and al-shahid's counterpart (i.e., they are two forms of the same root with the same sense). She withdrew far only to flee from her people, lest they reproach her for bearing a child without a husband.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her﴾. ʿIkrimah, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read ﴿al-mikhad﴾ with a kasra on the mim. al-Farra' said: The meaning is: the labour pains brought her, and when the particle (bi, "with") was removed, an alif was placed in the verb, similar to ﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾ [al-Kahf: 63], meaning "with our morning meal," and similar to ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], meaning "with blocks of iron." Abu 'Ubayda said: "ajā'ahā" is used of the one who came, and "ajā'a-hā" is used of someone else bringing her. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning is "he brought her and compelled her," from the expressions "need brought me to you" (jā'at bī al-ḥājatu ilayka) and "need compelled me to you" (ajā'atnī al-ḥājatu ilayka). al-Makhad means labour pains. Others said: al-makhad is the pain of childbirth.

﴿To the trunk of the palm tree﴾, which is the stem of the palm, and it was a dry palm standing in the desert, having neither a crown nor fronds.

﴿She said: "Oh, would that I had died before this"﴾, that is, before this day or this matter. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Hafs read ﴿mittu﴾ with a kasra on the mim.

There are two views on the reason for her saying this: One, she said it out of shame before people. The second, so that they would not sin by slandering her.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I had been a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿nasyan﴾ with a kasra on the nun. Hamzah and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿nasyan﴾ with a fatha on the nun. al-Farra' said: The companions of ʿAbd Allah read it with a fatha on the nun, while the rest of the Arabs read it with a kasra, and both are dialects, like al-jisr and al-jasr, and al-witr and al-wattr, and the fatha is more beloved to me. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: The kasra is according to both dialects. Ibn al-Anbari said: Whoever reads with a kasra says: al-nasy is a noun for what is forgotten, like al-bughd being a noun for what is hated, and al-sabb a noun for what is reviled. And al-nasy with a fatha is also a noun for what is forgotten, as a verbal noun that stands in place of the noun, as one says "al-rajul danif" and "danaf" (a sick man): the kasra form is the proper descriptive adjective, and the fatha form is a verbal noun that takes the place of the adjective. It is possible that al-nasy and al-nisy are two nouns with one meaning, as one says al-ritl and al-ratl (both meaning a pound).

The exegetes have five views regarding His saying: ﴿nasyan mansiyyan﴾: [p. 221]

First: "Would that I had not been anything." This was said by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿAta' and Ibn Zayd also said this.

Second: ﴿And I had been a thing forgotten﴾, that is, a discarded menstrual cloth. This was said by Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah. al-Farra' said: al-nasy is what a woman discards of her menstrual rags. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is the menstrual rags a woman throws away, which no one seeks or remembers.

Third: It is from miscarriage (al-saqt). This was said by Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Rabi'.

Fourth: The meaning is: "Would that I were unknown, and no one knew who I am." This was said by Qatada.

Fifth: It is a trivial thing that people leave behind on a journey, so it becomes insignificant to them and they do not return for it. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-nasy and al-mansiyy are what is forgotten of a water-skin or a staff, meaning that it is forgotten in the dwelling and no one returns for it, because its owner considers it worthless. al-Kisa'i said: The meaning of the verse is: "Would that I had been something which, when mentioned, would not be sought."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he called to her from below her﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a fatha on the mim and the ta'. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a kasra on the mim and the ta'. Whoever reads with a kasra on the mim has two interpretations: One: the angel called to her from beneath the palm tree. It was also said: she was on a raised ground, and the angel called to her from lower than her. The second: Jesus called to her when he came out of her womb. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Everything to which you raise your eye is above you, and everything to which you lower your eye is below you. Whoever reads with a fatha on the mim has the two interpretations mentioned. al-Farra' used to say: The one who addressed her was only the angel, according to both readings.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾. There are two views on this:

[p. 222] One: It is a small stream. This was said by the majority of exegetes and philologists. Abu Salih and Ibn Jurayj said: It is al-jadwal (a stream) in Syriac.

The second: It is Jesus, who was a "sariyy" (a noble, honoured one) among men. This was said by al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and [Ibn Zayd]. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Hasan retracted this view in favour of the first view. If it were a description of Jesus, he would be a "sariyy" youth or a "sawiyy" (a sound, upright one) among the boys, and the Arabs rarely say "I saw a noble with you" until they say "a noble man."

If it is asked: How does it fit her consolation that it was said: "Do not grieve, for here is a flowing stream"?

The answer has two aspects: One: She grieved over the barrenness of the place where she had given birth, the lack of food and drink, and the water with which to purify herself. So it was said: "Do not grieve, We have made a stream flow for you and caused fresh dates to fall for you." This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: She grieved over what had befallen her of bearing a child without a husband. So Allah, exalted is He, made a stream flow for her, which came to her from the Jordan, and brought forth dates for her from the dry tree, and that was a sign showing the power of Allah, exalted is He, in creating Jesus. This was said by Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And shake toward you﴾. Al-hazz means shaking.

The particle (bi, "with") in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the trunk of the palm tree﴾ has two views:

One: It is an additional, emphatic particle, like His saying: ﴿Let him extend a rope to the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]. al-Farra' said: The meaning is: "Let him extend a rope." The Arabs say: "hazzahu" and "hazza bihi" (both mean "he shook it"), and "khudh al-khitam" and "khudh bi-l-khitam" (both mean "take the halter"), and "ta'allaqa Zaydan" and "ta'allaqa bihi" (both mean "he clung to Zayd"). Abu ʿUbayda said: It is emphatic, like the saying of the poet:

*"We strike with the sword and hope for relief."*

[p. 223] The second: It entered the trunk to make it adhere to the shaking, so it is conveying attachment (ilsaq). This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿tusāqiṭ﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, al-Sakka'i and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ with a ta' and a doubled sin. Hamzah and ʿAbd al-Warith read ﴿tasāqaṭ﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a single sin. Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿tusāqiṭ﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the qaf, with a single sin. Ya'qub and Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal read ﴿yassāqaṭu﴾ with a fatha on the ya', a doubled sin, and a fatha on the qaf. These are the famous recitations. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu Haywa read ﴿taskutu﴾ with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the sin, and a damma on the qaf. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, ʿAisha and al-Hasan read ﴿yusāqiṭ﴾ with an alif, a single sin, a damma on the ya', and a kasra on the qaf. al-Dahhak and ʿAmr ibn Dinar read ﴿yusqiṭ﴾ with a damma on the ya', a kasra on the qaf, a sukun on the sin, and no alif. ʿAsim al-Jahdari and Abu ʿImran al-Jawni read the same, except with a ta'. Mu'adh al-Qari' and Ibn Ya'mur read the same, except with a nun. Abu Razin al-ʿUqaili and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿yasqut﴾ with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the sin, and a damma on the qaf. Abu al-Sammak al-ʿAdawi and Ibn Hizam read ﴿tatasāqaṭu﴾ with two fathas on the two ta's and an alif. al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads ﴿yassāqaṭ﴾, the meaning is ﴿yatasāqaṭ﴾, and the ta' was assimilated into the sin. Whoever reads ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ is the same, and used the feminine because the word "palm tree" (nakhla) is feminine. Whoever reads ﴿tasāqaṭ﴾ with a ta' and lightening, has removed from ﴿tatasāqaṭu﴾ the meeting of two ta's. Whoever reads ﴿yassāqaṭ﴾ intends the meaning: "the trunk fell down upon you." Whoever reads ﴿nusāqiṭ﴾ with a nun, the meaning is: "We shall cause it to fall upon you, and We make it a sign for you." The grammarians say: [p. 224] When you say ﴿yassāqaṭu﴾ or ﴿yatasāqaṭu﴾, ﴿ruṭaban﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The meaning is: "the trunk drops fresh dates." When you say ﴿tassāqaṭ﴾ with a ta', the meaning is: "the palm tree drops fresh dates."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿janiyyan﴾. al-Farra' said: al-janiyy means "that which is picked." Ibn al-Anbari said: It is the fresh one, and the original form is "mujnū", which was changed from the pattern of maf'ul to fa'il, as one says "qadid" and "tabikh" (dried meat and cooked meat). Others said: It is the fresh one with its dust still on it. That palm tree had no crown, so Allah, exalted is He, caused it to grow, and when she placed her hand upon it, the fresh dates fell, fresh. The early generations (al-salaf) used to recommend fresh dates for women after childbirth, because of Maryam, peace be upon her.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So eat﴾, that is, of the fresh dates, ﴿and drink﴾ from the stream, ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ by the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him. al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "qarirat bihi ʿaynan, aqarru" (with the fatha on the qaf in the imperfect), and "qarrarat fi al-makan, aqarru" (with the kasra on the qaf); and "ʿaynan" is in the accusative as a specification. Ibn al-Anbari related from al-Asma'i that he said: The meaning of ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ is: "let your tears be cooled," because tears of joy are cool, and tears of grief are hot. The derivation of "qarri" is from al-qarur, which is cold water. Ahmad ibn Yahya said to us: The explanation of "qarri ʿaynan" is: you have reached the goal of your hope, so that your eye is cooled from looking toward anything else, and he cited the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*"On a day of dread, with striking and thrusting, by which your clients' eyes were made content."*

That is, they achieved victory and reached the end of their hopes, so their eyes were cooled from looking to anything else.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you see﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, al-Dahhak, Abu al-ʿAliya and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read ﴿tara'inna﴾ with a kasra on the hamza and no ya'. That is: if you see any human being, then say. There is an implied element in it, its estimated meaning being: "then if he asks you about the matter of your child." ﴿Then say: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast"﴾. There are two views on this: [p. 225]

One: silence (ṣamt). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas ibn Malik and al-Dahhak. Likewise Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Anas ibn Malik and Abu Razin al-ʿUqaili read ﴿ṣamtan﴾ in place of "ṣawman" (fast). Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿ṣiyaman﴾.

The second meaning: fasting from food, drink and speech. This is what Qatadah said. Ibn Zayd said: the diligent worshipper among the Children of Israel would fast from speech just as he fasts from food, except for the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As-Suddi said: so Allah permitted her to speak only this much, and then she would remain silent. Ibn Mas'ud said: she was commanded to silence, because she had no proof before the people, so she was commanded to refrain from speech so that her son would suffice her in speaking, by clearing her good name. It was also said: she would speak with the angels but would not speak with mankind. Ibn al-Anbari said: the word sawm (fasting, in the sense of abstention) in the language of the Arabs has four meanings. It is said: sawm for abstaining from food and drink; sawm for silence; sawm for a kind of tree; and sawm for the dung of the ostrich.

The scholars differed over the age of Maryam on the day she gave birth, giving three opinions:

The first: she gave birth when she was fifteen years old. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The second: she was twelve years old. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: she was thirteen years old. This was said by Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verse 27–33:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, in the transmission of Abu Salih, said: "She brought him to them forty days after, when she had become pure from her postnatal bleeding (nifas)." And he said, in the transmission of al-Dahhak: "Her people set out seeking her, and when she saw them she carried ʿIsa and went out to meet them with him, and that is His saying: ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him.﴾"

If it is said: "*Then she brought him*" already conveys "*carrying him*," so there is no benefit in the repetition.

The answer: When signs had appeared from him, it was possible that the hearer would imagine, from "*then she brought him*," that he was walking on his own feet, so that his walking would be a sign like his speech. Therefore the phrase cut off this assumption and informed that he was like other infants. This is similar to the saying of the Arabs: "I looked at so-and-so with my eye," thereby negating a look of tenderness and mercy and affirming that it was a look of the eye itself.

Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "When she entered upon her people, they wept, for they were righteous people, and they said: ﴿O Maryam, you have certainly come with something monstrous (shay'an fariyyan).﴾" Regarding *fariyyan* there are three opinions:

One: a great thing. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah. Al-Farra' said: *al-fary* means the great. The Arabs say: "I left him *yafri al-fary*," meaning when he did a work and did it excellently, so that people surpass others in it. It is said of this... The Prophet ﷺ said: "I have not seen a *ʿabqari* (a man of genius) who *yafri* (performs) the *fary* of ʿUmar."

The second: a wondrous, extraordinary thing. This was said by Abu ʿUbaydah.

The third: a fabricated thing. From this comes the saying: "*faraytu al-kadhiba*" and "*iftaraytuhu*" (I invented the lie). This was said by al-Yazidi. (p. 227)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾. Regarding who is meant by Harun here there are five opinions:

One: he was her brother from her mother, and he was among the best youths of the Children of Israel. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Dahhak said: he was from her father and her mother.

The second: she was from the descendants of Harun. This was said by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Suddi said: she was from the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, peace be upon them both, and she was attributed to him because she was of his offspring.

The third: he was a righteous man among the Children of Israel, and they likened her to him in righteousness. This is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah, and what supports it is what al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah narrated, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent me to the people of Najran, and they said: 'Do you not recite: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾, and you know what was between Musa and ʿIsa?' I did not know how to answer them, so I returned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him. He said: 'Did you not tell them that they used to hear about their prophets and the righteous before them?'"

The fourth: the people of Harun included sinners and fornicators, so they attributed her to them. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: he was a man of the sinners of the Children of Israel whom they likened her to. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. (p. 228)

On this basis, two views emerge regarding the meaning of *"sister"* (ukht):

One: that she is literally a sister. The second: resemblance, not kinship, as in His saying: ﴿And We show them no sign except that it is greater than its sister﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 48].

His saying: ﴿Your father was not a man of evil﴾, meaning ʿImran, *(imra'a su')*: that is, an adulterer. ﴿Nor was your mother a woman unchaste (bagiyyan)﴾, that is, an adulteress. So from where is this child for you?

His saying: ﴿So she pointed to him﴾, that is, she gestured to him, toward ʿIsa, ﴿and he spoke.﴾ It was also said: the meaning is that she gestured to them to speak to him. ʿIsa had already spoken to her when she came to her people and said: "O mother, rejoice, for I am the servant of Allah and His Messiah." When she gestured that they should speak to him, they marvelled at that, and ﴿they said: How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?﴾ There are four opinions regarding *kana* here:

One: it is superfluous, so the meaning is: how can we speak to a child in the cradle?

The second: it means "came to be" and "happened."

The third: it has the meaning of a conditional and a consequent, so the meaning is: whoever is a child in the cradle, how can we speak to him? This was related by al-Zajjaj, who preferred this last view. Ibn al-Anbari said: this is like your saying: "How can I admonish one who does not accept my admonition?", that is, whoever does not accept. The past tense in the consequent takes the meaning of the future.

The fourth: that *kana* means "became" (sara). This was said by Qutrub.

Regarding the meaning of *al-mahd* (the cradle) there are two views: One: her lap, said by Nawf, Qatadah and al-Kalbi. The second: the well-known cradle of the infant, also related by al-Kalbi.

Al-Suddi said: When ʿIsa heard their words, he did nothing more than leave off suckling and turn toward them with his face, and said: ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah.﴾ The commentators said: He mentioned servanthood first only to nullify the claim of those who attributed lordship (rububiyyah) to him. (p. 229)

Regarding His saying: ﴿He has given me the Book﴾, Hamzah pronounced this ya' with sukun. Regarding the meaning of the verse there are two views:
