His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, in the transmission of Abu Salih, said: "She brought him to them forty days after, when she had become pure from her postnatal bleeding (nifas)." And he said, in the transmission of al-Dahhak: "Her people set out seeking her, and when she saw them she carried ʿIsa and went out to meet them with him, and that is His saying: ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him.﴾"

If it is said: "*Then she brought him*" already conveys "*carrying him*," so there is no benefit in the repetition.

The answer: When signs had appeared from him, it was possible that the hearer would imagine, from "*then she brought him*," that he was walking on his own feet, so that his walking would be a sign like his speech. Therefore the phrase cut off this assumption and informed that he was like other infants. This is similar to the saying of the Arabs: "I looked at so-and-so with my eye," thereby negating a look of tenderness and mercy and affirming that it was a look of the eye itself.

Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "When she entered upon her people, they wept, for they were righteous people, and they said: ﴿O Maryam, you have certainly come with something monstrous (shay'an fariyyan).﴾" Regarding *fariyyan* there are three opinions:

One: a great thing. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah. Al-Farra' said: *al-fary* means the great. The Arabs say: "I left him *yafri al-fary*," meaning when he did a work and did it excellently, so that people surpass others in it. It is said of this... The Prophet ﷺ said: "I have not seen a *ʿabqari* (a man of genius) who *yafri* (performs) the *fary* of ʿUmar."

The second: a wondrous, extraordinary thing. This was said by Abu ʿUbaydah.

The third: a fabricated thing. From this comes the saying: "*faraytu al-kadhiba*" and "*iftaraytuhu*" (I invented the lie). This was said by al-Yazidi. (p. 227)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾. Regarding who is meant by Harun here there are five opinions:

One: he was her brother from her mother, and he was among the best youths of the Children of Israel. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Dahhak said: he was from her father and her mother.

The second: she was from the descendants of Harun. This was said by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Suddi said: she was from the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, peace be upon them both, and she was attributed to him because she was of his offspring.

The third: he was a righteous man among the Children of Israel, and they likened her to him in righteousness. This is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah, and what supports it is what al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah narrated, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent me to the people of Najran, and they said: 'Do you not recite: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾, and you know what was between Musa and ʿIsa?' I did not know how to answer them, so I returned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him. He said: 'Did you not tell them that they used to hear about their prophets and the righteous before them?'"

The fourth: the people of Harun included sinners and fornicators, so they attributed her to them. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: he was a man of the sinners of the Children of Israel whom they likened her to. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. (p. 228)

On this basis, two views emerge regarding the meaning of *"sister"* (ukht):

One: that she is literally a sister. The second: resemblance, not kinship, as in His saying: ﴿And We show them no sign except that it is greater than its sister﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 48].

His saying: ﴿Your father was not a man of evil﴾, meaning ʿImran, *(imra'a su')*: that is, an adulterer. ﴿Nor was your mother a woman unchaste (bagiyyan)﴾, that is, an adulteress. So from where is this child for you?

His saying: ﴿So she pointed to him﴾, that is, she gestured to him, toward ʿIsa, ﴿and he spoke.﴾ It was also said: the meaning is that she gestured to them to speak to him. ʿIsa had already spoken to her when she came to her people and said: "O mother, rejoice, for I am the servant of Allah and His Messiah." One: it is superfluous, so the meaning is: how can we speak to a child in the cradle?

The second: it means "came to be" and "happened."

The third: it has the meaning of a conditional and a consequent, so the meaning is: whoever is a child in the cradle, how can we speak to him? This was related by al-Zajjaj, who preferred this last view. Ibn al-Anbari said: this is like your saying: "How can I admonish one who does not accept my admonition?", that is, whoever does not accept. The past tense in the consequent takes the meaning of the future.

The fourth: that *kana* means "became" (sara). This was said by Qutrub.

Regarding the meaning of *al-mahd* (the cradle) there are two views: One: her lap, said by Nawf, Qatadah and al-Kalbi. The second: the well-known cradle of the infant, also related by al-Kalbi.

Al-Suddi said: When ʿIsa heard their words, he did nothing more than leave off suckling and turn toward them with his face, and said: ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah.﴾ The commentators said: He mentioned servanthood first only to nullify the claim of those who attributed lordship (rububiyyah) to him. If it is said: "*Then she brought him*" already conveys "*carrying him*," so there is no benefit in the repetition.

The answer: When signs had appeared from him, it was possible that the hearer would imagine, from "*then she brought him*," that he was walking on his own feet, so that his walking would be a sign like his speech. The second: a wondrous, extraordinary thing. This was said by Abu ʿUbaydah.

The third: a fabricated thing. From this comes the saying: "*faraytu al-kadhiba*" and "*iftaraytuhu*" (I invented the lie). This was said by al-Yazidi. (p. 227)

Regarding the meaning of *"zakah"* there are two views: One: the zakah of wealth, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: purity, said by al-Zajjaj. (p. 230)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And dutiful to my mother﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when he said this, and did not say "to my father," they knew that he had been born without a human father.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He has not made me arrogant (jabbaran), wretched (shaqiyyan)﴾, that is, disobedient to his Lord. ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born﴾. The commentators said: safety from Allah is upon me the day I was born, so that no devil harmed me. The explanation of this verse has already passed [Maryam: 15].

If it is said: Why does he mention "*al-salam*" here with the definite article, while he mentioned it in the story of Yahya without the definite article? There are two answers regarding this:

One: since the mention of *salam* had occurred before this place without the definite article, it was better that it appear a second time with the definite article. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

This view has been objected to, it being said: how is it permissible to join this, which is the speech of ʿIsa, to the first, which is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic?

Ibn al-Anbari answered this, saying: ʿIsa only learns from his Lord, so it is permissible that he heard the speech of Allah concerning Yahya, built upon it and attached it to himself. It is also permissible that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, recognized the second *salam*, since it came after a *salam* He had mentioned, and applied it to it without intending to follow the quoted wording, since the speaker may alter some of the speech he reports. He says: "'Abd Allah said: I am a fair man," meaning: "'Abd Allah said to me: you are a fair man."

The second answer: *salam* and *al-salam* are two dialects with one meaning, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

(p-231) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, the one who said, ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah﴾, is the son of Mary, not as the Christians say: that he is the son of Allah and that he is God.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the word of truth﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (qawlu al-haqqi) with a raised lam (ḍamm). 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the lam (naṣb). Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "qawlu al-haqq" with the raised lam, the meaning is: he is the word of truth, meaning this statement; and whoever reads it with the fatha, the meaning is: I say the word of truth. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two possibilities regarding the verse:

One of them: since he was described as "the word" (kalimah), it was permissible to describe him as "speech" (qawl).

The second: there is an implied element in the sentence, its estimate being: that is the report about Jesus; that report is the word of truth.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿about which they dispute﴾; that is, they doubt. Qatadah said: The Jews and the Christians disputed about him. The Jews claimed that he was a sorcerer, and the Christians claimed that he was the son of Allah and the third of three. Abu Mijlaz, Mu'adh al-Qari', Ibn Ya'mar and Abu Raja' read (tamtarun) with a ta' at the beginning.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is not for Allah to take any son﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: to take a son. The "min" (min) here is emphatic, indicating the negation of one and of many; for the speaker may say, "I have not taken a horse," meaning he has taken more than that; and he may say, (p-232) "I have not taken two horses or more," meaning he has taken one horse. But when he says, "I have not taken any horse (min faras)," this indicates the negation of one and of all.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Be, and it is﴾. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read (fayakuna) with a fatha. We have already mentioned its explanation in (al-Baqarah: 117).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed Allah is my Lord and your Lord﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read (wa-anna Allaha) with a fatha on the alif. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (wa-inna Allaha) with a kasra on the alif. This is from the speech of Jesus. Whoever reads with a fatha takes it as conjoined to his saying: ﴿and He has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah﴾ and [that] Allah is my Lord; whoever reads with a kasra has two possibilities:

One of them: that it is conjoined to his saying: ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah﴾.

The second: that it is a new independent sentence.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verse 37–40:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then the factions differed among themselves﴾. The exegetes said: "min" (among) is superfluous, and the meaning is: they differed among themselves. Ibn al-Anbari said: When the believers held fast to the truth, the difference of the factions was confined to them.

Regarding "the factions" there are two opinions:

One: they are the Jews and the Christians. The Jews said that he (Jesus) was born out of lawful wedlock, while the Christians claimed concerning him what does not befit him.

(p-233) The second: they are the sects of the Christians. Some of them said: He is God; some said: He is the son of God; and some said: He is the third of three.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved﴾ by their saying concerning the Messiah, ﴿from the scene of a great Day﴾; that is, from their presence on that Day for the recompense.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How clearly they will hear and see [on the Day they come to Us]﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: its wording is that of a command, but its meaning is a report. So the meaning is: How much they will hear and how much they will see on the Day of Resurrection! They heard and saw when that did not benefit them, because they witnessed of the command of God what made them need no reflection or thought; so they knew the guidance and obeyed. This is the saying of the majority.

The second: "Hear of their words today and see how He deals with them on the Day ﴿when they come to Us﴾." This was said by Abu al-Aliyah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But the wrongdoers are today in clear error﴾; that is, the polytheists and the disbelievers, ﴿today﴾, that is, in this world, ﴿are in clear error﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And warn them﴾; that is, frighten the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿of the Day of Regret﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection, when the evildoer regrets that he did not do good, and the negligent regrets that he did not increase in goodness.

The causes of regret on the Day of Resurrection are many. Among them is what Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, it will be said: O people of Paradise! So they will crane their necks and look. And it will be said: O people of the Fire! So they will crane their necks and look. Then Death will be brought in the form of a horned ram, white with black spots, and it will be said to them: Do you recognize this? (p-234) They will say: This is Death. It will be slaughtered, and then it will be said: O people of Paradise, eternity without death; and O people of the Fire, eternity without death." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will have been decided while they are in heedlessness and they do not believe.﴾"

The exegetes said: This is the regret, when Death is slaughtered. If anyone were to die of joy, the people of Paradise would die; and if anyone were to die of grief, the people of the Fire would die.

Among the causes of regret is what 'Adi ibn Hatim narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection, people will be brought to Paradise, until when they draw near to it, and smell its fragrance, and look at its palaces, it will be called out: Turn them away from it, we have no share for them in it. So they will return with a regret such as the first ones did not return with its like. They will say: Our Lord, if You had admitted us to the Fire before You showed us what You have shown us, it would have been easier for us. He will say: That is what I intended for you. When you were alone, you challenged Me with great sins; and when you met people, you met them humbly, showing people what is contrary to what you give Me from your hearts. You revered people and did not revere Me; you honored people and did not honor Me; you left things for people and did not leave them for Me. So today I will make you taste the punishment, along with what I have deprived you of in reward."

Among the causes of regret is what has been related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: No soul on the Day of Resurrection will fail to look at a house in Paradise and a house in the Fire. Then it will be said – meaning to these: "If only you had done good," and to the people of Paradise: "Had it not been that God bestowed His favor upon you."

(p-235)

Among the causes of regret is the cutting off of hope when the Fire closes over its people.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When the matter is decided﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Qudiya" in the language means: it was perfected and firmly established. The judge was called "qadi" only because of his perfecting and firmly establishing what he executes. In the verse there is an ellipsis, and the meaning is: when the matter is decided in which is their destruction.

Regarding "the matter," the exegetes have two opinions:

One: it is the slaughtering of Death, said by Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi. The second: the meaning is: the punishment has been decreed for them, said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿While they are in heedlessness﴾; that is, they are in the world, in heedlessness of what will be done to them on that Day, ﴿and they do not believe﴾ in what will happen in the Hereafter.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We inherit the earth and whoever is upon it, and to Us they will be returned﴾; that is, We cause its inhabitants to die and then We inherit it, ﴿and to Us they will be returned﴾ after death.

If it is asked: What is the benefit of "Nahnu" (We) when "Inna" (Indeed) already suffices for it?

The answer: Since in the speech of one who magnifies himself, "Inna naf'alu" (Indeed We do) could give the impression that his followers did the act, "Nahnu" makes clear that the act is truly attributed to Him.

If it is asked: Why did He say ﴿and whoever is upon it﴾, when He inherits humans and others?

The answer: "Man" is specific to those who can discern, while those who cannot discern enter into the sense of "the earth" and are treated as its category. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both answers to the two questions.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verse 37–40:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then the factions differed among themselves﴾. The exegetes said: "min" (among) is superfluous, and the meaning is: they differed among themselves. Ibn al-Anbari said: When the believers held fast to the truth, the difference of the factions was confined to them.

Regarding "the factions" there are two opinions:

One: they are the Jews and the Christians. The Jews said that he (Jesus) was born out of lawful wedlock, while the Christians claimed concerning him what does not befit him.

(p-233) The second: they are the sects of the Christians. Some of them said: He is God; some said: He is the son of God; and some said: He is the third of three.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved﴾ by their saying concerning the Messiah, ﴿from the scene of a great Day﴾; that is, from their presence on that Day for the recompense.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How clearly they will hear and see [on the Day they come to Us]﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: its wording is that of a command, but its meaning is a report. So the meaning is: How much they will hear and how much they will see on the Day of Resurrection! They heard and saw when that did not benefit them, because they witnessed of the command of God what made them need no reflection or thought; so they knew the guidance and obeyed. This is the saying of the majority.

The second: "Hear of their words today and see how He deals with them on the Day ﴿when they come to Us﴾." This was said by Abu al-Aliyah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But the wrongdoers are today in clear error﴾; that is, the polytheists and the disbelievers, ﴿today﴾, that is, in this world, ﴿are in clear error﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And warn them﴾; that is, frighten the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿of the Day of Regret﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection, when the evildoer regrets that he did not do good, and the negligent regrets that he did not increase in goodness.

The causes of regret on the Day of Resurrection are many. Among them is what Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, it will be said: O people of Paradise! So they will crane their necks and look. And it will be said: O people of the Fire! So they will crane their necks and look. Then Death will be brought in the form of a horned ram, white with black spots, and it will be said to them: Do you recognize this? (p-234) They will say: This is Death. It will be slaughtered, and then it will be said: O people of Paradise, eternity without death; and O people of the Fire, eternity without death." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will have been decided while they are in heedlessness and they do not believe.﴾"

The exegetes said: This is the regret, when Death is slaughtered. If anyone were to die of joy, the people of Paradise would die; and if anyone were to die of grief, the people of the Fire would die.

Among the causes of regret is what 'Adi ibn Hatim narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection, people will be brought to Paradise, until when they draw near to it, and smell its fragrance, and look at its palaces, it will be called out: Turn them away from it, we have no share for them in it. So they will return with a regret such as the first ones did not return with its like. They will say: Our Lord, if You had admitted us to the Fire before You showed us what You have shown us, it would have been easier for us. He will say: That is what I intended for you. When you were alone, you challenged Me with great sins; and when you met people, you met them humbly, showing people what is contrary to what you give Me from your hearts. You revered people and did not revere Me; you honored people and did not honor Me; you left things for people and did not leave them for Me. So today I will make you taste the punishment, along with what I have deprived you of in reward."

Among the causes of regret is what has been related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: No soul on the Day of Resurrection will fail to look at a house in Paradise and a house in the Fire. Then it will be said – meaning to these: "If only you had done good," and to the people of Paradise: "Had it not been that God bestowed His favor upon you."

Among the causes of regret is the cutting off of hope when the Fire closes over its people.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verse 41–50:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham﴾; that is, recount to your people his story. The meaning of ṣiddīq (truthful one) has already been discussed under [An-Nisa: 69].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and it will not avail you anything﴾; that is, it will not repel any harm from you.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, there has come to me of knowledge﴾ of Allah and recognition ﴿that which has not come to you﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾; that is, do not obey him in what he commands of disbelief and sins. We have already explained the meaning of "kāna" earlier. And ʿaṣiyy means ʿāṣin (disobedient); it is faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, I fear that there will touch you a punishment from the Most Merciful﴾. Muqatil said: in the Hereafter. Others said: in this world. ﴿And you would be to Satan a companion﴾; that is, an associate in the punishment of Allah, so companionship has taken the place of allegiance. It has been said: Abraham only hoped for his father's faith because, when he came out of the fire, he said to him: "How excellent is your god, O Abraham." Then he began to advise him, and his father replied: ﴿Do you dislike my gods, O Abraham?﴾; that is, are you abandoning their worship? ﴿If you do not desist﴾ from denouncing them and reviling them, ﴿I will surely stone you﴾. There are two opinions regarding this:

One: with insult and speech; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

The second: with stones, until you distance yourself from me; this was said by al-Hasan.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And leave me alone for a long time﴾. There are two opinions regarding this:

One: leave me for a long time. It was related by Maymun ibn Mihran from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan, al-Farra' and most of them said the same. Ibn Qutaybah said: "Leave me for a long period of time"; and from this is said: "tamallaytu ḥabībaka" (I enjoyed the company of your beloved for a long time).

The second: keep away from me unharmed before my punishment reaches you. It was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Qatadah and al-Dahhak said the same. In this case it is from their saying: "Fulan is mallī' with such-and-such" (meaning he is capable of it), so the meaning is: leave me while your honour is intact and you are safe from my harm. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: Peace be upon you﴾; that is, you are safe from my inflicting any harm upon you, because he had not been commanded to fight him over his disbelief. ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾. There are two opinions regarding this:

One: the meaning is: I will ask Allah for a repentance through which you may attain His forgiveness.

The second: that he promised him forgiveness while not knowing that this is forbidden for those who persist in disbelief. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, He has ever been to me Ḥafiyy (gracious)﴾. There are three opinions regarding this:

One: Latif (kind), related by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Zayd and al-Zajjaj said the same.

The second: Raḥīm (merciful), related by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: Barr (benevolent), who accustomed me to answering when I call upon Him; this was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I will leave you﴾; that is, I will withdraw from you, and I will leave ﴿what you call upon besides Allah﴾, meaning the idols.

Regarding the meaning of "tadʿūn" (you call upon) there are two opinions:

One: you worship.

The second: the meaning is: what you call upon as lord. ﴿And I will call upon my Lord﴾; that is, I will worship Him, ﴿perhaps I will not be in my supplication to my Lord unhappy﴾; that is, I hope I will not be made wretched by His worship as you have been made wretched by the worship of idols, because they do not benefit them nor respond to their supplication. ﴿So when he had removed himself from them﴾. The commentators said: he migrated away from them to the land of Syria, and Allah granted him Isaac and Jacob, and Allah consoled his loneliness at being separated from his people with noble offspring. Abu Sulayman said: He granted him Isaac and Jacob after Ishmael.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And each﴾; that is, each of these two. Muqatil said: "And each" refers to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, ﴿We made a prophet﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We gave them of Our mercy﴾. The commentators said: wealth and children, and knowledge and action. ﴿And We made for them a tongue of truthfulness, exalted﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, a good and elevated remembrance among people; so all the people of the religions befriend Abraham and his offspring and praise them, and the tongue was put in place of speech, because speech is by means of the tongue.

One: leave me for a long time. It was related by Maymun ibn Mihran from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan, al-Farra' and most of them said the same. Ibn Qutaybah said: "Leave me for a long period of time"; and from this is said: "tamallaytu ḥabībaka" (I enjoyed the company of your beloved for a long time).

The second: keep away from me unharmed before my punishment reaches you. It was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Qatadah and al-Dahhak said the same. In this case it is from their saying: "Fulan is mallī' with such-and-such" (meaning he is capable of it), so the meaning is: leave me while your honour is intact and you are safe from my harm. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: Peace be upon you﴾; that is, you are safe from my inflicting any harm upon you, because he had not been commanded to fight him over his disbelief. ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾. There are two opinions regarding this:

One: the meaning is: I will ask Allah for a repentance through which you may attain His forgiveness.

The second: that he promised him forgiveness while not knowing that this is forbidden for those who persist in disbelief. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, He has ever been to me Ḥafiyy (gracious)﴾. There are three opinions regarding this:

One: Latif (kind), related by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Zayd and al-Zajjaj said the same.

The second: Raḥīm (merciful), related by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: Barr (benevolent), who accustomed me to answering when I call upon Him; this was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I will leave you﴾; that is, I will withdraw from you, and I will leave ﴿what you call upon besides Allah﴾, meaning the idols.

Regarding the meaning of "tadʿūn" (you call upon) there are two opinions:

One: you worship.

The second: the meaning is: what you call upon as lord. ﴿And I will call upon my Lord﴾; that is, I will worship Him, ﴿perhaps I will not be in my supplication to my Lord unhappy﴾; that is, I hope I will not be made wretched by His worship as you have been made wretched by the worship of idols, because they do not benefit them nor respond to their supplication. ﴿So when he had removed himself from them﴾. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And each﴾; that is, each of these two. Muqatil said: "And each" refers to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, ﴿We made a prophet﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We gave them of Our mercy﴾. The commentators said: wealth and children, and knowledge and action. ﴿And We made for them a tongue of truthfulness, exalted﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, a good and elevated remembrance among people; so all the people of the religions befriend Abraham and his offspring and praise them, and the tongue was put in place of speech, because speech is by means of the tongue.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he was sincere﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read *mukhlisan* with a kasra on the lam. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read it with a fatha on the lam.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-mukhlis* (with a kasra on the lam) is the one who declared God's oneness and made himself purely devoted to obeying God, free of any impurity. *Al-mukhlas* (with a fatha on the lam) is the one whom God chose and made a chosen person, pure and free of any impurity.

Among their speech is "on the right of the qibla" and "on its left," by which they mean the side to the right and left of one who faces it. The exegetes said: the call came from the right of Moses, which is why He said "the right," and by it He did not mean the right side of the mountain.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verses 54–57:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, he was true to his promise﴾. This is general, concerning what was between him and Allah and what was between him and the people. Mujahid said: "He never promised his Lord anything except that he fulfilled it."

If it is asked: "How did He single out Isma'il for being true to his promise, when there are prophets who are not like this?"

The answer: Isma'il endured in fulfilling a promise what other prophets did not endure, so He praised him for that. The exegetes (mufassirun) mentioned that he had an appointment with a man, and he waited for him for a period. There are three opinions about that period:

The first: he waited a full year, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: twenty-two days, said by al-Ruqashi. The third: three days, said by Muqatil.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And he was a messenger﴾ to his people, who were Jurhum. ﴿And he used to enjoin on his family﴾. Muqatil said: "That means his people." Al-Zajjaj said: "His family: all of his community (ummah)." As for prayer (salah) and zakat, they are the two well-known acts of worship. (p-241)

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We raised him to a high station﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

The first: that he is in the fourth heaven. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the two Sahihs narrated from the hadith of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the hadith of the Mi'raj (Night Ascension), that he saw Idris in the fourth heaven. This was also said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Mujahid, and Abu al-'Aliyah.

The second: that he is in the sixth heaven. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak said it.

The third: that he is in Paradise (al-Jannah). Zayd ibn Aslam said it. This returns to the first opinion, because it has been narrated that Paradise is in the fourth heaven.

The fourth: that he is in the seventh heaven. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi related it.

Concerning the reason for his ascent to the heaven, there are three opinions:

The first: that more of his deeds used to be raised up than were raised up for all the children of Adam. So the Angel of Death (Malak al-Mawt) loved him and asked Allah for permission to be his friend (khullah), and He permitted him. He descended to him in the form of a human being, and he accompanied him. When Idris recognized him, he said: "I ask you for something." He said: "What is it?" He said: "Let me taste death, so that I may know its severity, and be better prepared for it." So Allah revealed to him that he should take his soul for an hour and then release him. He did so, then said: "How did you find it?" He said: "It was harder than what I had heard about it. I would love for you to show me the Fire." So he carried him and showed him it. He said: "I would love for you to show me Paradise," and he showed it to him. When he entered it he walked around in it. The Angel of Death said to him: "Come out." He said: "By Allah, I will not come out until Allah the Exalted brings me out." So Allah sent an angel who judged between them. He said: "What do you say, O Angel of Death?" So he related what had happened. Then he said: "What do you say, O Idris?" He said: "Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185], and I have tasted it. He said: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass through it﴾ [Maryam: 71], and I have passed through it. And He said to the people of Paradise: ﴿And they will never be removed from it﴾ [al-Hijr: 48]. By Allah, I will not come out until Allah brings me out." Then he heard a voice from above him saying: "By My permission he entered, and by My command he acted; so release him." This is the meaning of what Zayd ibn Aslam narrated, traced back (marfu') to the Prophet (ﷺ).

If a questioner asks: "From where did Idris have these verses, when they are in our Book?" Ibn al-Anbari mentioned from some scholars that Allah the Exalted had informed Idris of what is mentioned in the Qur'an about the inevitability of arrival (at Hell), the impossibility of leaving Paradise, and other things, so he said what he said with knowledge.

The second: that an angel from among the angels asked his Lord for permission to descend to Idris, and He permitted him. When Idris recognized him, he said: "Is there any kinship between you and the Angel of Death?" He said: "He is my brother among the angels." He said: "Can you intercede for me with the Angel of Death?" He said: "I will speak to him about you (p-243) so that he will be gentle with you. Ride between my wings." Idris rode, and he ascended with him to the heaven. He met the Angel of Death and said: "I have a need of you." He said: "I know your need: you want me to speak about Idris, and his name has been erased from the register, and there remains of his term only the blink of an eye." So Idris died between the wings of the angel. This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Salih said from Ibn 'Abbas: "So the Angel of Death took the soul of Idris in the sixth heaven."

The third: that Idris walked one day in the sun, and its heat struck him. He said: "O Allah, lighten its burden on the one who carries it," meaning the angel appointed over the sun. When the angel woke up he found a lightness and heat from the sun that he did not recognize, so he asked Allah the Mighty and Majestic about that. He said: "My servant Idris asked Me to lighten its burden and heat upon you, and I answered him." The angel said: "My Lord, bring me together with him and make between us a friendship (khullah)." So He permitted him, and he came to him. Among what Idris said to him was: "Intercede for me with the Angel of Death so that he delays my term." He said: "Allah does not delay a soul when its term has come. But I will speak to him about you. What he was not able to do for anyone among the children of Adam, he will do for you." Then the angel carried him on his wing and raised him to the heaven, and placed him at the rising place of the sun. Then he came to the Angel of Death and said: "I have a need of you, the need of a friend of mine from the children of Adam. You intercede for me with him so that you delay his term." He said: "That is not for me. But if you wish, I will inform him when he will die." He looked in his register and said: "You spoke to me about a man whom I do not see dying ever, and I do not find him dying except at the rising place of the sun." He said: "I came to you and left him there." He said: "Go, for I do not think you will find him except dead. By Allah, nothing remains of his term." So the angel returned and found him dead. This meaning is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b, among others. This report and the one before it indicate that he is dead, while the first opinion indicates that he is alive. (p-244)

He said: "I know your need: you want me to speak about Idris, and his name has been erased from the register, and there remains of his term only the blink of an eye." So Idris died between the wings of the angel. This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Salih said from Ibn 'Abbas: "So the Angel of Death took the soul of Idris in the sixth heaven."

The third: that Idris walked one day in the sun, and its heat struck him. He said: "O Allah, lighten its burden on the one who carries it," meaning the angel appointed over the sun. When the angel woke up he found a lightness and heat from the sun that he did not recognize, so he asked Allah the Mighty and Majestic about that. He said: "My servant Idris asked Me to lighten its burden and heat upon you, and I answered him." The angel said: "My Lord, bring me together with him and make between us a friendship (khullah)." So He permitted him, and he came to him. Among what Idris said to him was: "Intercede for me with the Angel of Death so that he delays my term." He said: "Allah does not delay a soul when its term has come. But I will speak to him about you. What he was not able to do for anyone among the children of Adam, he will do for you." Then the angel carried him on his wing and raised him to the heaven, and placed him at the rising place of the sun. Then he came to the Angel of Death and said: "I have a need of you, the need of a friend of mine from the children of Adam. You intercede for me with him so that you delay his term." He said: "That is not for me. But if you wish, I will inform him when he will die." He looked in his register and said: "You spoke to me about a man whom I do not see dying ever, and I do not find him dying except at the rising place of the sun." He said: "I came to you and left him there." He said: "Go, for I do not think you will find him except dead. By Allah, nothing remains of his term." So the angel returned and found him dead. This meaning is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b, among others. This report and the one before it indicate that he is dead, while the first opinion indicates that he is alive. (p-244)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verses 54–57:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, he was true to his promise﴾. This is general, concerning what was between him and Allah and what was between him and the people. Mujahid said: "He never promised his Lord anything except that he fulfilled it."

If it is asked: "How did He single out Isma'il for being true to his promise, when there are prophets who are not like this?"

The answer: Isma'il endured in fulfilling a promise what other prophets did not endure, so He praised him for that. The exegetes (mufassirun) mentioned that he had an appointment with a man, and he waited for him for a period. There are three opinions about that period:

The first: he waited a full year, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: twenty-two days, said by al-Ruqashi. The third: three days, said by Muqatil.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And he was a messenger﴾ to his people, who were Jurhum. ﴿And he used to enjoin on his family﴾. Muqatil said: "That means his people." Al-Zajjaj said: "His family: all of his community (ummah)." As for prayer (salah) and zakat, they are the two well-known acts of worship. (p-241)

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We raised him to a high station﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

The first: that he is in the fourth heaven. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the two Sahihs narrated from the hadith of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the hadith of the Mi'raj (Night Ascension), that he saw Idris in the fourth heaven. This was also said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Mujahid, and Abu al-'Aliyah.

The second: that he is in the sixth heaven. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak said it.

The third: that he is in Paradise (al-Jannah). Zayd ibn Aslam said it. This returns to the first opinion, because it has been narrated that Paradise is in the fourth heaven.

The fourth: that he is in the seventh heaven. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi related it.

Concerning the reason for his ascent to the heaven, there are three opinions:

The first: that more of his deeds used to be raised up than were raised up for all the children of Adam. So the Angel of Death (Malak al-Mawt) loved him and asked Allah for permission to be his friend (khullah), and He permitted him. He descended to him in the form of a human being, and he accompanied him. When Idris recognized him, he said: "I ask you for something." He said: "What is it?" He said: "Let me taste death, so that I may know its severity, and be better prepared for it." So Allah revealed to him that he should take his soul for an hour and then release him. He did so, then said: "How did you find it?" He said: "It was harder than what I had heard about it. I would love for you to show me the Fire." So he carried him and showed him it. He said: "I would love for you to show me Paradise," and he showed it to him. When he entered it he walked around in it. The Angel of Death said to him: "Come out." He said: "By Allah, I will not come out until Allah the Exalted brings me out." So Allah sent an angel who judged between them. He said: "What do you say, O Angel of Death?" So he related what had happened. Then he said: "What do you say, O Idris?" He said: "Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185], and I have tasted it. He said: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass through it﴾ [Maryam: 71], and I have passed through it. And He said to the people of Paradise: ﴿And they will never be removed from it﴾ [al-Hijr: 48]. By Allah, I will not come out until Allah brings me out." Then he heard a voice from above him saying: "By My permission he entered, and by My command he acted; so release him." This is the meaning of what Zayd ibn Aslam narrated, traced back (marfu') to the Prophet (ﷺ).

If a questioner asks: "From where did Idris have these verses, when they are in our Book?" Ibn al-Anbari mentioned from some scholars that Allah the Exalted had informed Idris of what is mentioned in the Qur'an about the inevitability of arrival (at Hell), the impossibility of leaving Paradise, and other things, so he said what he said with knowledge.

The second: that an angel from among the angels asked his Lord for permission to descend to Idris, and He permitted him. When Idris recognized him, he said: "Is there any kinship between you and the Angel of Death?" He said: "He is my brother among the angels." He said: "Can you intercede for me with the Angel of Death?" He said: "I will speak to him about you (p-243) so that he will be gentle with you. Ride between my wings." Idris rode, and he ascended with him to the heaven. He met the Angel of Death and said: "I have a need of you." He said: "I know your need: you want me to speak about Idris, and his name has been erased from the register, and there remains of his term only the blink of an eye." So Idris died between the wings of the angel. This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Salih said from Ibn 'Abbas: "So the Angel of Death took the soul of Idris in the sixth heaven."

The third: that Idris walked one day in the sun, and its heat struck him. He said: "O Allah, lighten its burden on the one who carries it," meaning the angel appointed over the sun. When the angel woke up he found a lightness and heat from the sun that he did not recognize, so he asked Allah the Mighty and Majestic about that. He said: "My servant Idris asked Me to lighten its burden and heat upon you, and I answered him." The angel said: "My Lord, bring me together with him and make between us a friendship (khullah)." So He permitted him, and he came to him. Among what Idris said to him was: "Intercede for me with the Angel of Death so that he delays my term." He said: "Allah does not delay a soul when its term has come. But I will speak to him about you. What he was not able to do for anyone among the children of Adam, he will do for you." Then the angel carried him on his wing and raised him to the heaven, and placed him at the rising place of the sun. Then he came to the Angel of Death and said: "I have a need of you, the need of a friend of mine from the children of Adam. You intercede for me with him so that you delay his term." He said: "That is not for me. But if you wish, I will inform him when he will die." He looked in his register and said: "You spoke to me about a man whom I do not see dying ever, and I do not find him dying except at the rising place of the sun." He said: "I came to you and left him there." He said: "Go, for I do not think you will find him except dead. By Allah, nothing remains of his term." So the angel returned and found him dead. This meaning is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b, among others. This report and the one before it indicate that he is dead, while the first opinion indicates that he is alive. (p-244)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are they upon whom Allah bestowed His favor from among the prophets﴾, meaning those whom He mentioned from among the prophets in this surah. ﴿Of the descendants of Adam﴾, meaning Idris. ﴿And of those whom We carried with Noah﴾, meaning Ibrahim, because he was of the offspring of Sam son of Noah. ﴿And of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾, meaning Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub. ﴿And Israel﴾, meaning and of the descendants of Israel, and they are Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And of those whom We guided﴾, that is, these were among those whom We guided aright. ﴿And chose﴾, that is, and selected.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They fell down prostrating﴾. al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Prostrating﴾ is a presumed circumstantial accusative (ḥāl muqaddarah, a circumstance that is anticipated rather than simultaneous). The meaning is: they fell down intending to prostrate, because a person, at the moment of falling, is not yet prostrating. (p. 245) So ﴿sujjadan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial term, and it is the plural of sājid (prostrating). ﴿And weeping﴾ is coordinated with it, and it is the plural of bākin (weeping). Thus Allah, Exalted is He, made clear that when the prophets heard the signs of Allah they would prostrate and weep out of fear of Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾. We have explained it in (al-A'raf: 169). Regarding the intended meaning of this succession there are three opinions:

The first: they are the Jews. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the Jews and the Christians. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: they are from this Ummah, who will come when the righteous of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) have passed away, competing in fornication, leaping upon one another in the alleys as fornicators. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They neglected the prayer﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Razin al-'Uqayli and al-Hasan al-Basri read ﴿al-salawat﴾ (the prayers) in the plural.

Regarding the meaning of their neglecting it there are two opinions:

The first: they delayed it beyond its time. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymirah.

The second: they abandoned it. This was said by al-Qurazi, and al-Zajjaj chose it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And followed their desires﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: That is like listening to singing, drinking wine, fornication, frivolity, and whatever resembles that which cuts one off from performing the obligations of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they will encounter error (ghayy)﴾. This encountering does not mean merely seeing; rather, what is intended is meeting and being involved with it together with seeing. (p. 246)

Regarding the meaning of this ghayy there are six opinions:

The first: it is a valley in Hell. This was narrated by Ibn 'Abbas from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Ka'b said likewise. The second: it is a river in Hell. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. The third: it is loss. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: it is punishment. This was said by Mujahid. The fifth: it is evil. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Sa'ib. The sixth: the meaning is: they will encounter the recompense of error, like His saying: ﴿He will encounter sin﴾ (al-Furqan: 68), that is, the recompense of sins. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except one who repents and believes﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: he repents from shirk and believes in Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Muqatil.

The second: he repents from neglecting the prayer and believes from among the Jews and the Christians.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, al-Dahhak, Ibn Ya'mur and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿Jannatu﴾ with a raised ta' (Jannatu 'Adnin, in the nominative). Al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Sha'bi and Ibn al-Sumayf'a read ﴿Jannatu 'Adnin﴾ in the singular with a raised ta'. Abu Mijlaz and Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji read ﴿Jannata 'Adnin﴾ in the singular with an accusative ta'. His saying: ﴿Which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen﴾, that is, He promised them it while they had not seen it, so it is absent from them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass (ma'tiyyan)﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: it means coming (ātiyan). Ibn Qutaybah said: It is a maf'ul (passive form) in the sense of fa'il (active form), and it is rare for the active sense to come in the form of the passive. Al-Farra' said: He only said ātiyan not ma'tiyyan because everything that comes to you, you come to it. Do you not see that you say: "I came upon fifty years," and "fifty years came upon me"?

The second: it means reached (mablughan ilayh). This was said by Ibn al-Anbari. Ibn Jurayj said: ﴿His promise﴾ here means what is promised, which is Paradise, and ﴿coming﴾ means that His friends come to it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: it is mutual accusation while drinking wine. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: it is whatever is idle in speech and for which one is held sinful. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: Al-laghw in Arabic is what is corrupt and discarded.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except the word "Peace" (salaman)﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: Peace is not part of idle talk, and the Arabs make an exception of something after something that is not of its kind. This is because they imply within it, so the meaning is: except that they hear therein peace. Ibn al-Anbari said: He made an exception of peace from what is not of its kind, and in that is an emphasis of the intended meaning, because if they hear from idle talk nothing but peace, then they hear no idle talk at all. Likewise His saying: ﴿Indeed, they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ (al-Shu'ara: 77), since none of their enmity toward me comes from other than the Lord of the worlds, so all of them are enemies.

Regarding the meaning of this peace there are two opinions:

The first: it is the angels' greeting of them. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: they hear nothing except what greets them with peace, and they do not hear what makes them sinful. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾. The exegetes said: There is no morning or evening in Paradise, but they are brought their provision, according to the measure of what they used to know, at dawn and in the evening. al-Hasan said: The Arabs did not know anything of life better than the morning meal and the evening meal, so Allah mentioned that to them. Qatadah said: When one of the Arabs obtained a morning meal and an evening meal, he was pleased with it, so Allah informed them that they have their provision in Paradise morning and evening according to the measure of that time, and there is no night nor day there, but only light and radiance. al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated that he said: I asked Zuhayr ibn Muhammad about His saying: ﴿Morning and evening﴾, and he said: There is no night nor day in Paradise. They are always in light, and they have a measure of night and day: they know the measure of night by the lowering of curtains and the closing of doors, and they know the measure of day by the raising of curtains and the opening of doors.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is the Paradise﴾. The demonstrative refers to His saying: ﴿So those will enter Paradise﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Which We cause to inherit (nurith)﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Qatadah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with a fathah on the waw and a shaddah on the ra'. The exegetes said: The meaning of ﴿nurith﴾ is: We give to the believers the dwellings that would have belonged to the people of the Fire had they believed. It is also permissible that the meaning of "nurith" is: We give, so it is like an inheritance for them from the standpoint that it is a new ownership. We have explained this in (al-A'raf: 43).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾. Ibn al-Sumayf'a and Ibn Ya'mur read ﴿wa-ma yatanazzalu﴾ with a fathah on the ya'.

Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions:

The first: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Jibril, what prevents you from visiting us more than you visit us?' So this verse was revealed." This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. (p. 249)

The second: "The angel was late in coming to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then he came to him, and he said: 'Perhaps I was late.' He said: 'You have indeed.' He said: 'And why would I not, when you do not use the siwak, nor trim your fingernails, nor cleanse your barājim?' So the verse was revealed." This was said by Mujahid. Ibn al-Anbari said: The barājim in the language of the Arabs are the knuckles that are at the joints of the finger-bones, which appear when the fingers are clenched and are hidden when they are spread out. The rawājib are what lies between the barājim, and between every two knuckles there is a rājibah.

The third: "Jibril was detained from the Prophet (ﷺ) when his people asked him about the story of the People of the Cave, Dhu al-Qarnayn, and the Spirit, and he did not know what to answer them, and he hoped that Jibril would bring him an answer. So he was delayed, and that caused the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) great hardship. When Jibril descended, he said to him: 'You were late with me until my thoughts became bad and I longed for you.' Jibril said: 'I was indeed eager, but I am a servant who is commanded. When I am sent, I descend, and when I am held back, I am held back.' So this verse was revealed." This was said by 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Regarding the cause of Jibril's detention from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there are two opinions:

The first: because of his companions' refusal to observe full cleanliness, as we mentioned in the hadith of Mujahid.

The second: because they asked him about the story of the People of the Cave, and he said: "Tomorrow I will inform you," and he did not say: "If Allah wills." This has already been mentioned in (al-Kahf: 24).

Regarding the length of his detention from him there are five opinions:

The first: fifteen days, which we have mentioned in (al-Kahf) from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: forty days. This was said by 'Ikrimah and Muqatil. The third: twelve nights. This was said by Mujahid. The fourth: three days. This was related by Muqatil. The fifth: twenty-five days. (p. 250) This was related by al-Tha'labi. It was also said that Surah al-Duha was revealed on account of this occasion.

The exegetes hold that His saying: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ is the statement of Jibril. al-Mawardi related that it is the statement of the people of Paradise when they enter it, so the meaning is: we do not enter these gardens except by the command of Allah. It was also said: we do not descend to any place in Paradise except by the command of Allah.

Regarding His saying: ﴿That which is before us and that which is behind us﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: "That which is before us" is the Hereafter, and "that which is behind us" is this world. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and Muqatil said likewise.

The second: "That which is before us" is what has passed of this world, and "that which is behind us" is of the Hereafter. This is the reverse of the first, and it was said by Mujahid. al-Akhfash said: "That which is before us" is before we were created, and "that which is behind us" is after annihilation.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what is between that﴾ there are three opinions:

The first: what is between this world and the Hereafter. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: what is between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). This was said by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Abu al-'Aliyah.

The third: since He created us. This was said by al-Akhfash. Ibn al-Anbari said: He used the singular for that, while the reference is to two things: "that which is before us" and "that which is behind us," because the Arabs use that for two and for the plural.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful (nasiyyan)﴾. Nasiyy here means the same as nasi (forgetful).

Regarding the meaning of the statement there are two opinions:

The first: He never abandoned you since the revelation was delayed from you. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: He did not forget you at the cessation of the revelation from you. (p. 251)

The second: He is knowing of what was and what will be, and He forgets nothing. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So worship Him﴾, that is, affirm His oneness (tawhid, the affirmation of Allah's unity), because worshipping Him with shirk is not worship. ﴿And be steadfast in His worship﴾, that is, be patient in affirming His oneness. It was also said: in obeying His command and avoiding His prohibition.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ Harun narrated from Abu 'Amr that he used to assimilate the lam of ﴿hal ta'lamu﴾ (idghām, assimilation of consonants). Its basis is that Sibawayh permits the assimilation of the lam into the ta', tha', dal, zay, sin, sad and ta', because the last point of articulation of the lam is close to their points of articulation. Abu 'Ubaydah said: When a ta' follows "hal," there are two dialects: some make the lam of "hal" clear, and some assimilate it.

Regarding the meaning of the statement there are three opinions:

The first: an equal and a likeness. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatadah said likewise.

The second: do you know anyone else named "Allah" besides Him? This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: do you know anyone who deserves to be called "Creator" and "Capable" except Him? This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Sha'bi and Ibn al-Sumayf'a read ﴿Jannatu 'Adnin﴾ in the singular with a raised ta'. Abu Mijlaz and Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji read ﴿Jannata 'Adnin﴾ in the singular with an accusative ta'. His saying: ﴿Which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen﴾, that is, He promised them it while they had not seen it, so it is absent from them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass (ma'tiyyan)﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: it means coming (ātiyan). Ibn Qutaybah said: It is a maf'ul (passive form) in the sense of fa'il (active form), and it is rare for the active sense to come in the form of the passive. Al-Farra' said: He only said ātiyan not ma'tiyyan because everything that comes to you, you come to it. Do you not see that you say: "I came upon fifty years," and "fifty years came upon me"?

The second: it means reached (mablughan ilayh). This was said by Ibn al-Anbari. Ibn Jurayj said: ﴿His promise﴾ here means what is promised, which is Paradise, and ﴿coming﴾ means that His friends come to it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: it is mutual accusation while drinking wine. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: it is whatever is idle in speech and for which one is held sinful. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: Al-laghw in Arabic is what is corrupt and discarded.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except the word "Peace" (salaman)﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: Peace is not part of idle talk, and the Arabs make an exception of something after something that is not of its kind. This is because they imply within it, so the meaning is: except that they hear therein peace. Ibn al-Anbari said: He made an exception of peace from what is not of its kind, and in that is an emphasis of the intended meaning, because if they hear from idle talk nothing but peace, then they hear no idle talk at all. Likewise His saying: ﴿Indeed, they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ (al-Shu'ara: 77), since none of their enmity toward me comes from other than the Lord of the worlds, so all of them are enemies.

Regarding the meaning of this peace there are two opinions:

The first: it is the angels' greeting of them. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: they hear nothing except what greets them with peace, and they do not hear what makes them sinful. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾. The exegetes said: There is no morning or evening in Paradise, but they are brought their provision, according to the measure of what they used to know, at dawn and in the evening. al-Hasan said: The Arabs did not know anything of life better than the morning meal and the evening meal, so Allah mentioned that to them. Qatadah said: When one of the Arabs obtained a morning meal and an evening meal, he was pleased with it, so Allah informed them that they have their provision in Paradise morning and evening according to the measure of that time, and there is no night nor day there, but only light and radiance. al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated that he said: I asked Zuhayr ibn Muhammad about His saying: ﴿Morning and evening﴾, and he said: There is no night nor day in Paradise. They are always in light, and they have a measure of night and day: they know the measure of night by the lowering of curtains and the closing of doors, and they know the measure of day by the raising of curtains and the opening of doors.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is the Paradise﴾. The demonstrative refers to His saying: ﴿So those will enter Paradise﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Which We cause to inherit (nurith)﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Qatadah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with a fathah on the waw and a shaddah on the ra'. The exegetes said: The meaning of ﴿nurith﴾ is: We give to the believers the dwellings that would have belonged to the people of the Fire had they believed. It is also permissible that the meaning of "nurith" is: We give, so it is like an inheritance for them from the standpoint that it is a new ownership. We have explained this in (al-A'raf: 43).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾. Ibn al-Sumayf'a and Ibn Ya'mur read ﴿wa-ma yatanazzalu﴾ with a fathah on the ya'.

Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions:

The first: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Jibril, what prevents you from visiting us more than you visit us?' So this verse was revealed." This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. (p. 249)

The second: "The angel was late in coming to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then he came to him, and he said: 'Perhaps I was late.' He said: 'You have indeed.' He said: 'And why would I not, when you do not use the siwak, nor trim your fingernails, nor cleanse your barājim?' So the verse was revealed." This was said by Mujahid. Ibn al-Anbari said: The barājim in the language of the Arabs are the knuckles that are at the joints of the finger-bones, which appear when the fingers are clenched and are hidden when they are spread out. The rawājib are what lies between the barājim, and between every two knuckles there is a rājibah.

The third: "Jibril was detained from the Prophet (ﷺ) when his people asked him about the story of the People of the Cave, Dhu al-Qarnayn, and the Spirit, and he did not know what to answer them, and he hoped that Jibril would bring him an answer. So he was delayed, and that caused the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) great hardship. When Jibril descended, he said to him: 'You were late with me until my thoughts became bad and I longed for you.' Jibril said: 'I was indeed eager, but I am a servant who is commanded. When I am sent, I descend, and when I am held back, I am held back.' So this verse was revealed." This was said by 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Regarding the cause of Jibril's detention from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there are two opinions:

The first: because of his companions' refusal to observe full cleanliness, as we mentioned in the hadith of Mujahid.

The second: because they asked him about the story of the People of the Cave, and he said: "Tomorrow I will inform you," and he did not say: "If Allah wills." This has already been mentioned in (al-Kahf: 24).

Regarding the length of his detention from him there are five opinions:

The first: fifteen days, which we have mentioned in (al-Kahf) from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: forty days. This was said by 'Ikrimah and Muqatil. The third: twelve nights. This was said by Mujahid. The fourth: three days. This was related by Muqatil. The fifth: twenty-five days. (p. 250) This was related by al-Tha'labi. It was also said that Surah al-Duha was revealed on account of this occasion.

The exegetes hold that His saying: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ is the statement of Jibril. al-Mawardi related that it is the statement of the people of Paradise when they enter it, so the meaning is: we do not enter these gardens except by the command of Allah. It was also said: we do not descend to any place in Paradise except by the command of Allah.

Regarding His saying: ﴿That which is before us and that which is behind us﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: "That which is before us" is the Hereafter, and "that which is behind us" is this world. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and Muqatil said likewise.

The second: "That which is before us" is what has passed of this world, and "that which is behind us" is of the Hereafter. This is the reverse of the first, and it was said by Mujahid. al-Akhfash said: "That which is before us" is before we were created, and "that which is behind us" is after annihilation.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what is between that﴾ there are three opinions:

The first: what is between this world and the Hereafter. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: what is between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). This was said by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Abu al-'Aliyah.

The third: since He created us. This was said by al-Akhfash. Ibn al-Anbari said: He used the singular for that, while the reference is to two things: "that which is before us" and "that which is behind us," because the Arabs use that for two and for the plural.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful (nasiyyan)﴾. Nasiyy here means the same as nasi (forgetful).

Regarding the meaning of the statement there are two opinions:

The first: He never abandoned you since the revelation was delayed from you. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: He did not forget you at the cessation of the revelation from you. (p. 251)

The second: He is knowing of what was and what will be, and He forgets nothing. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So worship Him﴾, that is, affirm His oneness (tawhid, the affirmation of Allah's unity), because worshipping Him with shirk is not worship. ﴿And be steadfast in His worship﴾, that is, be patient in affirming His oneness. It was also said: in obeying His command and avoiding His prohibition.

Its basis is that Sibawayh permits the assimilation of the lam into the ta', tha', dal, zay, sin, sad and ta', because the last point of articulation of the lam is close to their points of articulation. Abu 'Ubaydah said: When a ta' follows "hal," there are two dialects: some make the lam of "hal" clear, and some assimilate it.

Regarding the meaning of the statement there are three opinions:

The first: an equal and a likeness. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatadah said likewise.

The second: do you know anyone else named "Allah" besides Him? This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: do you know anyone who deserves to be called "Creator" and "Capable" except Him? This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And of those whom We guided﴾, that is, these were among those whom We guided aright. ﴿And chose﴾, that is, and selected.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They fell down prostrating﴾. al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Prostrating﴾ is a presumed circumstantial accusative (ḥāl muqaddarah, a circumstance that is anticipated rather than simultaneous). The meaning is: they fell down intending to prostrate, because a person, at the moment of falling, is not yet prostrating. (p. 245) So ﴿sujjadan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial term, and it is the plural of sājid (prostrating). ﴿And weeping﴾ is coordinated with it, and it is the plural of bākin (weeping). Thus Allah, Exalted is He, made clear that when the prophets heard the signs of Allah they would prostrate and weep out of fear of Allah.

The first: they are the Jews. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the Jews and the Christians. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: they are from this Ummah, who will come when the righteous of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) have passed away, competing in fornication, leaping upon one another in the alleys as fornicators. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They neglected the prayer﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Razin al-'Uqayli and al-Hasan al-Basri read ﴿al-salawat﴾ (the prayers) in the plural.

Regarding the meaning of their neglecting it there are two opinions:

The first: they delayed it beyond its time. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymirah.

The second: they abandoned it. This was said by al-Qurazi, and al-Zajjaj chose it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And followed their desires﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: That is like listening to singing, drinking wine, fornication, frivolity, and whatever resembles that which cuts one off from performing the obligations of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they will encounter error (ghayy)﴾. This encountering does not mean merely seeing; rather, what is intended is meeting and being involved with it together with seeing. (p. 246)

The third: it is loss. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: it is punishment. This was said by Mujahid. The fifth: it is evil. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Sa'ib. The first: he repents from shirk and believes in Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Muqatil.

The second: he repents from neglecting the prayer and believes from among the Jews and the Christians.

The first: it is a valley in Hell. This was narrated by Ibn 'Abbas from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Ka'b said likewise. The second: it is a river in Hell. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. The third: it is loss. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: it is punishment. This was said by Mujahid. The fifth: it is evil. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Sa'ib. The sixth: the meaning is: they will encounter the recompense of error, like His saying: ﴿He will encounter sin﴾ (al-Furqan: 68), that is, the recompense of sins. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except one who repents and believes﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: he repents from shirk and believes in Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Muqatil.

The second: he repents from neglecting the prayer and believes from among the Jews and the Christians.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, al-Dahhak, Ibn Ya'mur and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿Jannatu﴾ with a raised ta' (Jannatu 'Adnin, in the nominative). Al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Sha'bi and Ibn al-Sumayf'a read ﴿Jannatu 'Adnin﴾ in the singular with a raised ta'. Abu Mijlaz and Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji read ﴿Jannata 'Adnin﴾ in the singular with an accusative ta'. His saying: ﴿Which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen﴾, that is, He promised them it while they had not seen it, so it is absent from them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass (ma'tiyyan)﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: it means coming (ātiyan). Ibn Qutaybah said: It is a maf'ul (passive form) in the sense of fa'il (active form), and it is rare for the active sense to come in the form of the passive. The second: it means reached (mablughan ilayh). This was said by Ibn al-Anbari. Ibn Jurayj said: ﴿His promise﴾ here means what is promised, which is Paradise, and ﴿coming﴾ means that His friends come to it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: it is mutual accusation while drinking wine. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: it is whatever is idle in speech and for which one is held sinful. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: Al-laghw in Arabic is what is corrupt and discarded.

The second: they hear nothing except what greets them with peace, and they do not hear what makes them sinful. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: He is knowing of what was and what will be, and He forgets nothing. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The first: they are the Jews. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the Jews and the Christians. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: they are from this Ummah, who will come when the righteous of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) have passed away, competing in fornication, leaping upon one another in the alleys as fornicators. The second: they abandoned it. This was said by al-Qurazi, and al-Zajjaj chose it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And followed their desires﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: That is like listening to singing, drinking wine, fornication, frivolity, and whatever resembles that which cuts one off from performing the obligations of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
