The second: do you know anyone else named "Allah" besides Him? This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: do you know anyone who deserves to be called "Creator" and "Capable" except Him? This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are they upon whom Allah bestowed His favor from among the prophets﴾, meaning those whom He mentioned from among the prophets in this surah. ﴿Of the descendants of Adam﴾, meaning Idris. ﴿And of those whom We carried with Noah﴾, meaning Ibrahim, because he was of the offspring of Sam son of Noah. ﴿And of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾, meaning Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub. ﴿And Israel﴾, meaning and of the descendants of Israel, and they are Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And of those whom We guided﴾, that is, these were among those whom We guided aright. ﴿And chose﴾, that is, and selected.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They fell down prostrating﴾. al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Prostrating﴾ is a presumed circumstantial accusative (ḥāl muqaddarah, a circumstance that is anticipated rather than simultaneous). The meaning is: they fell down intending to prostrate, because a person, at the moment of falling, is not yet prostrating. (p. 245) So ﴿sujjadan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial term, and it is the plural of sājid (prostrating). ﴿And weeping﴾ is coordinated with it, and it is the plural of bākin (weeping). Thus Allah, Exalted is He, made clear that when the prophets heard the signs of Allah they would prostrate and weep out of fear of Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾. We have explained it in (al-A'raf: 169). Regarding the intended meaning of this succession there are three opinions:

The first: they are the Jews. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the Jews and the Christians. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: they are from this Ummah, who will come when the righteous of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) have passed away, competing in fornication, leaping upon one another in the alleys as fornicators. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They neglected the prayer﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Razin al-'Uqayli and al-Hasan al-Basri read ﴿al-salawat﴾ (the prayers) in the plural.

Regarding the meaning of their neglecting it there are two opinions:

The first: they delayed it beyond its time. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymirah.

The second: they abandoned it. This was said by al-Qurazi, and al-Zajjaj chose it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And followed their desires﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: That is like listening to singing, drinking wine, fornication, frivolity, and whatever resembles that which cuts one off from performing the obligations of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they will encounter error (ghayy)﴾. This encountering does not mean merely seeing; rather, what is intended is meeting and being involved with it together with seeing. (p. 246)

Regarding the meaning of this ghayy there are six opinions:

The first: it is a valley in Hell. This was narrated by Ibn 'Abbas from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Ka'b said likewise. The second: it is a river in Hell. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. The third: it is loss. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: it is punishment. This was said by Mujahid. The fifth: it is evil. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Sa'ib. The sixth: the meaning is: they will encounter the recompense of error, like His saying: ﴿He will encounter sin﴾ (al-Furqan: 68), that is, the recompense of sins. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except one who repents and believes﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: he repents from shirk and believes in Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Muqatil.

The second: he repents from neglecting the prayer and believes from among the Jews and the Christians.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, al-Dahhak, Ibn Ya'mur and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿Jannatu﴾ with a raised ta' (Jannatu 'Adnin, in the nominative). Al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Sha'bi and Ibn al-Sumayf'a read ﴿Jannatu 'Adnin﴾ in the singular with a raised ta'. Abu Mijlaz and Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji read ﴿Jannata 'Adnin﴾ in the singular with an accusative ta'. His saying: ﴿Which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen﴾, that is, He promised them it while they had not seen it, so it is absent from them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass (ma'tiyyan)﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: it means coming (ātiyan). Ibn Qutaybah said: It is a maf'ul (passive form) in the sense of fa'il (active form), and it is rare for the active sense to come in the form of the passive. Al-Farra' said: He only said ātiyan not ma'tiyyan because everything that comes to you, you come to it. Do you not see that you say: "I came upon fifty years," and "fifty years came upon me"?

The second: it means reached (mablughan ilayh). This was said by Ibn al-Anbari. Ibn Jurayj said: ﴿His promise﴾ here means what is promised, which is Paradise, and ﴿coming﴾ means that His friends come to it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: it is mutual accusation while drinking wine. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: it is whatever is idle in speech and for which one is held sinful. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: Al-laghw in Arabic is what is corrupt and discarded.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except the word "Peace" (salaman)﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: Peace is not part of idle talk, and the Arabs make an exception of something after something that is not of its kind. This is because they imply within it, so the meaning is: except that they hear therein peace. Ibn al-Anbari said: He made an exception of peace from what is not of its kind, and in that is an emphasis of the intended meaning, because if they hear from idle talk nothing but peace, then they hear no idle talk at all. Likewise His saying: ﴿Indeed, they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ (al-Shu'ara: 77), since none of their enmity toward me comes from other than the Lord of the worlds, so all of them are enemies.

Regarding the meaning of this peace there are two opinions:

The first: it is the angels' greeting of them. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: they hear nothing except what greets them with peace, and they do not hear what makes them sinful. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾. The exegetes said: There is no morning or evening in Paradise, but they are brought their provision, according to the measure of what they used to know, at dawn and in the evening. al-Hasan said: The Arabs did not know anything of life better than the morning meal and the evening meal, so Allah mentioned that to them. Qatadah said: When one of the Arabs obtained a morning meal and an evening meal, he was pleased with it, so Allah informed them that they have their provision in Paradise morning and evening according to the measure of that time, and there is no night nor day there, but only light and radiance. al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated that he said: I asked Zuhayr ibn Muhammad about His saying: ﴿Morning and evening﴾, and he said: There is no night nor day in Paradise. They are always in light, and they have a measure of night and day: they know the measure of night by the lowering of curtains and the closing of doors, and they know the measure of day by the raising of curtains and the opening of doors.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is the Paradise﴾. The demonstrative refers to His saying: ﴿So those will enter Paradise﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Which We cause to inherit (nurith)﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Qatadah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with a fathah on the waw and a shaddah on the ra'. The exegetes said: The meaning of ﴿nurith﴾ is: We give to the believers the dwellings that would have belonged to the people of the Fire had they believed. It is also permissible that the meaning of "nurith" is: We give, so it is like an inheritance for them from the standpoint that it is a new ownership. We have explained this in (al-A'raf: 43).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾. Ibn al-Sumayf'a and Ibn Ya'mur read ﴿wa-ma yatanazzalu﴾ with a fathah on the ya'.

Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions:

The first: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Jibril, what prevents you from visiting us more than you visit us?' So this verse was revealed." This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. (p. 249)

The second: "The angel was late in coming to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then he came to him, and he said: 'Perhaps I was late.' He said: 'You have indeed.' He said: 'And why would I not, when you do not use the siwak, nor trim your fingernails, nor cleanse your barājim?' So the verse was revealed." This was said by Mujahid. Ibn al-Anbari said: The barājim in the language of the Arabs are the knuckles that are at the joints of the finger-bones, which appear when the fingers are clenched and are hidden when they are spread out. The rawājib are what lies between the barājim, and between every two knuckles there is a rājibah.

The third: "Jibril was detained from the Prophet (ﷺ) when his people asked him about the story of the People of the Cave, Dhu al-Qarnayn, and the Spirit, and he did not know what to answer them, and he hoped that Jibril would bring him an answer. So he was delayed, and that caused the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) great hardship. When Jibril descended, he said to him: 'You were late with me until my thoughts became bad and I longed for you.' Jibril said: 'I was indeed eager, but I am a servant who is commanded. When I am sent, I descend, and when I am held back, I am held back.' So this verse was revealed." This was said by 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Regarding the cause of Jibril's detention from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there are two opinions:

The first: because of his companions' refusal to observe full cleanliness, as we mentioned in the hadith of Mujahid.

The second: because they asked him about the story of the People of the Cave, and he said: "Tomorrow I will inform you," and he did not say: "If Allah wills." This has already been mentioned in (al-Kahf: 24).

Regarding the length of his detention from him there are five opinions:

The first: fifteen days, which we have mentioned in (al-Kahf) from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: forty days. This was said by 'Ikrimah and Muqatil. The third: twelve nights. This was said by Mujahid. The fourth: three days. This was related by Muqatil. The fifth: twenty-five days. (p. 250) This was related by al-Tha'labi. It was also said that Surah al-Duha was revealed on account of this occasion.

The exegetes hold that His saying: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ is the statement of Jibril. al-Mawardi related that it is the statement of the people of Paradise when they enter it, so the meaning is: we do not enter these gardens except by the command of Allah. It was also said: we do not descend to any place in Paradise except by the command of Allah.

Regarding His saying: ﴿That which is before us and that which is behind us﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: "That which is before us" is the Hereafter, and "that which is behind us" is this world. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and Muqatil said likewise.

The second: "That which is before us" is what has passed of this world, and "that which is behind us" is of the Hereafter. This is the reverse of the first, and it was said by Mujahid. al-Akhfash said: "That which is before us" is before we were created, and "that which is behind us" is after annihilation.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what is between that﴾ there are three opinions:

The first: what is between this world and the Hereafter. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: what is between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). This was said by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Abu al-'Aliyah.

The third: since He created us. This was said by al-Akhfash. Ibn al-Anbari said: He used the singular for that, while the reference is to two things: "that which is before us" and "that which is behind us," because the Arabs use that for two and for the plural.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful (nasiyyan)﴾. Nasiyy here means the same as nasi (forgetful).

Regarding the meaning of the statement there are two opinions:

The first: He never abandoned you since the revelation was delayed from you. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: He did not forget you at the cessation of the revelation from you. (p. 251)

The second: He is knowing of what was and what will be, and He forgets nothing. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So worship Him﴾, that is, affirm His oneness (tawhid, the affirmation of Allah's unity), because worshipping Him with shirk is not worship. ﴿And be steadfast in His worship﴾, that is, be patient in affirming His oneness. It was also said: in obeying His command and avoiding His prohibition.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ Harun narrated from Abu 'Amr that he used to assimilate the lam of ﴿hal ta'lamu﴾ (idghām, assimilation of consonants). Its basis is that Sibawayh permits the assimilation of the lam into the ta', tha', dal, zay, sin, sad and ta', because the last point of articulation of the lam is close to their points of articulation. Abu 'Ubaydah said: When a ta' follows "hal," there are two dialects: some make the lam of "hal" clear, and some assimilate it.

Regarding the meaning of the statement there are three opinions:

The first: an equal and a likeness. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatadah said likewise.

The second: do you know anyone else named "Allah" besides Him? This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: do you know anyone who deserves to be called "Creator" and "Capable" except Him? This was said by al-Zajjaj.

[p. 252] Allah's words: ﴿And man says﴾. The occasion of revelation of this verse: Ubayy ibn Khalaf took an old, decayed bone, began crumbling it in his hand and scattering it into the wind, and said: "Muhammad claims for you that Allah will resurrect us after we have become like this decayed bone." So this verse was revealed. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas. Ata narrated from Ibn Abbas that it was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

Allah's words: ﴿Shall I really be brought out alive?﴾ If it is asked: its apparent form is that of a question, so where is its answer? On this, Ibn al-Anbari mentions three answers:

The first: the apparent form of the speech is interrogative, but its meaning is one of denial and rejection. Its summary: "I am not going to be resurrected after death."

The second: when he asked this question about resurrection, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, answered him with His words: ﴿Does man not remember?﴾ So it contains the meaning of "Yes, you will be resurrected."

The third: the answer to the question of this disbeliever is in (Ya-Sin 36:78), at His words: ﴿And he strikes for Us a parable﴾, and it is not denied after the answer, because the whole Qur'an is like a single message, and the two surahs are Meccan.

Allah's words: ﴿Does man not remember?﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read yadhkuru with a fatha on the dhal and a shadda on the kaf. Nafi', Asim and Ibn Amir read (yadhkuru) with a sukun on the dhal and light (without shadda). Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji read (a-wa-la yatadhakkaru al-insan) with a ya and a ta. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and al-Hasan read (yadhkuru) with a ya and no ta, with a sukun on the dhal, light, and a damma on the kaf. The meaning: "Does this denier not remember his first creation, so that the beginning is taken as evidence for the return?"

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾, meaning: those who denied the resurrection, ﴿and the devils﴾, i.e., together with the devils, because every disbeliever is gathered with his devil in a chain. ﴿Then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees﴾ [p. 253]. Muqatil said: meaning, in Hell. For around something may be inside it: one says "the people sat around the house" when they sat inside it, encircling it. It was also said: they will crouch around it before they enter it.

As for His words ﴿on their knees (jithiyyan)﴾, al-Zajjaj said: it is the plural of jathin, like qa'id and qu'ud (sitter and sitters). It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. The original form has a damma on the jim, but it came with a kasra on it by assimilation to the kasra on the tha'.

The commentators have five opinions on its meaning:

The first: sitting, narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. The second: in groups, groups, also narrated from Ibn Abbas. On this view it is the plural of jathwa, which is a heap of earth and stones gathered together. The third: on their knees, said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Zajjaj. The fourth: standing, said by Abu Malik. The fifth: standing on their knees, said by al-Suddi, because of the narrowness of the place for them.

Allah's words: ﴿Then We will surely drag out from every sect﴾, i.e., We will take from every group, nation, and people of a religion, ﴿whichever of them was most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., the greatest of them in disobedience toward Him. The meaning: punishment begins with the most defiant, then the next most defiant, and with those greatest in crime and the leaders in evil. Al-Zajjaj said: regarding the nominative case of ayyuhum (whichever of them) there are three opinions:

The first: it is a fresh beginning, and "la-nanzi'anna" (We will surely drag out) has not governed anything. This is the view of Yunus.

The second: it is according to the sense of "those who are told to them: 'Which of them is most insolent toward the Most Merciful?'" This was said by al-Khalil and chosen by al-Zajjaj. He said: the interpretation is: "We will surely drag out the one who, because of his insolence..." It is said: "Which of these is most insolent?" And he recited a line [p. 254]:

"Indeed I spend the night away from the girl in a dwelling, so I spend the night neither troubled nor deprived."

The meaning: I spend the night like one of whom it is said: "He is neither troubled nor deprived."

The third: ayyuhum is built on a damma because it differs from its sisters. The meaning: "Which of them is the best?" The way it differs from its sisters is that you say "Strike whichever is best," but it is not good to say "Strike whoever is best" until you say "whoever is the best," and it is not good to say "Eat what is best" until you say "what is the best," nor "Take what is best" until you say "the one who is the best." So since "ma," "man," and "alladhi" differ from it, it was built on a damma. This was said by Sibawayh.

Allah's words: ﴿Then indeed We are most knowing of those most deserving of burning therein﴾. The meaning: the ones most deserving of burning therein are those who are most insolent, so they will be begun with before their followers. "Saliyyan" is in the accusative as a specification. It is said: "salia al-nar yaslaha" (he burned in the fire), when he entered it and endured its heat.

Allah's words: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾. There is an implied element in the speech; its estimate: "And there is none of you but he will pass over it."

Concerning who is intended by this address there are two opinions:

One: it is general concerning both the believer and the disbeliever. This is the view of the majority. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: this verse is for the disbelievers, but most of the narrations from him are like the first view. Ibn al-Anbari said: the reasoning for this is that when He said ﴿We will surely bring them﴾ and said ﴿whichever of them was most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾, the estimate was: "And there is none of them," so the kaf was replaced by the ha', as is done in His words: ﴿Indeed this was a reward for you﴾ (al-Insan 76:22), meaning "for them," because it refers back to His words ﴿and their Lord gave them to drink﴾ (al-Insan 76:21). A poet said:

"The lovers' places of visit have grown distant, so your pursuit of me, daughter of Makhram, has become hard on me."

He meant: your pursuit of her. On this passing over there are five opinions:

The first: it is entering. Jabir ibn Abd Allah narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Passing over is entering. Neither the righteous nor the wicked will remain who do not enter it. It will be cool and safe for the believer, as it was for Ibrahim, so much so that the Fire, or he said Hell, will cry out from their coolness." It was narrated from Ibn Abbas that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him about this verse, and he said to him: "As for you and me, we will enter it. So look: will Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bring us out of it or not?" He argued with His words: ﴿So He brought them to the Fire﴾ (Hud 11:98) and with His words: ﴿You and what you worship are fuel for Hell; you are going to it as passers-by﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:98). Abd Allah ibn Rawahah used to weep and say: "I have been told that I will pass over it, but I have not been told that I will come out from it." Al-Hasan al-Basri related that a man said to his brother: "O my brother, has it reached you that you will pass over the Fire?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Has it reached you that you will come out of it?" He said: "No." He said: "Then why laugh?" Khalid ibn Ma'dan said: when the people of Paradise enter Paradise they will say: "Did not our Lord promise us that we would pass over the Fire?" They will be told: "Yes, but you passed by it while it was extinguished."

Among those who held that it means entering are al-Hasan in one report, and Abu Malik. [p. 256] Objections have been raised against the proponents of this view on several grounds. Al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs say "I came to the land of such-and-such" and "I came to the water of such-and-such" when they approach it even if they do not enter, and from this is His words: ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan﴾ (al-Qasas 28:23). The decisive proof in this view is His words: ﴿Those will be kept far from it, they will not hear its faintest sound﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:101-102). Zuhayr said:

"When they came to the water, its pools blue, they set down the staves of the settled, encamped people."

That is, when they reached the water they stood over it.

I say: some of them have answered these arguments, saying: as for the first verse, when Musa stayed until he drew water and watered the sheep, his staying and his handling of it was as if he had entered. As for the other verse, it contains reports about the people of Paradise when they are in it, and then they will not hear its faintest sound. We have already related above from Khalid ibn Ma'dan that they pass by it and do not know it.

The second: passing over it means passing across it. This was said by Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah. Ibn Mas'ud said: people pass over the Fire, then they come out from it according to their deeds. The first of them will be like the flash of lightning, then like the wind, then like the running of a horse, [then like a rider on his mount], then like the tightening of the saddle, then like his walking.

The third: their passing over it means their presence at it. This was said by Ubayd ibn Umayr.

The fourth: the passing over of the Muslims means crossing the bridge, and the passing over of the polytheists means entering it. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: the believer's passing over it is what afflicts him of fever in this world. Uthman ibn al-Aswad narrated from Mujahid that he said: fever is every believer's share of the Fire. Then he recited: "And there is none of you but will pass over it." On this view, whoever among the Muslims has a fever has passed over it.

Allah's words: ﴿It is a decree binding upon your Lord﴾, meaning: the passing over, ﴿decided﴾. Hatm means making the judgment obligatory and cutting the matter off. The one decreed is the one Allah has decreed. The meaning: He made it binding and decreed it upon creation.

Allah's words: ﴿Then We will save those who were mindful of God﴾. Ibn Abbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn Yamur, Ibn Abi Layla, and Asim al-Jahdari read (thamma) with a fatha on the tha'. Al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read (nunji) with light pronunciation. Aisha, Abu Bahriyya, and Abu al-Jawza al-Rab'i read (thumma yunji) with a ya that is raised before the nun, light on the jim, and kasra. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn al-Sumayfa, and Abu Raja read (nunahhi) with an unpointed ha' and a shadda. This verse is used as evidence by those who say that all creation will enter it, because rescue (najah) is the extraction of one who has fallen into a thing. This is reinforced by His words: ﴿And We will leave the wrongdoers therein﴾, and He did not say "We will admit them." One says "nadhara" and "natruku" (we leave) only of one who has already been in his place. Whoever says that passing over is for the disbelievers alone says: the meaning of this speech is: "We will bring out the God-conscious from among those who enter the Fire." By "the God-conscious" are meant those who avoided polytheism, and by "the wrongdoers" are meant the disbelievers. The meaning of His words ﴿on their knees﴾ (Maryam 19:68) has already been mentioned.

[p. 252] Allah's words: ﴿And man says﴾. The occasion of revelation of this verse: Ubayy ibn Khalaf took an old, decayed bone, began crumbling it in his hand and scattering it into the wind, and said: "Muhammad claims for you that Allah will resurrect us after we have become like this decayed bone." So this verse was revealed. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas. Ata narrated from Ibn Abbas that it was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

Allah's words: ﴿Shall I really be brought out alive?﴾ If it is asked: its apparent form is that of a question, so where is its answer? On this, Ibn al-Anbari mentions three answers:

The first: the apparent form of the speech is interrogative, but its meaning is one of denial and rejection. Its summary: "I am not going to be resurrected after death."

The second: when he asked this question about resurrection, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, answered him with His words: ﴿Does man not remember?﴾ So it contains the meaning of "Yes, you will be resurrected."

The third: the answer to the question of this disbeliever is in (Ya-Sin 36:78), at His words: ﴿And he strikes for Us a parable﴾, and it is not denied after the answer, because the whole Qur'an is like a single message, and the two surahs are Meccan.

Allah's words: ﴿Does man not remember?﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read yadhkuru with a fatha on the dhal and a shadda on the kaf. Nafi', Asim and Ibn Amir read (yadhkuru) with a sukun on the dhal and light (without shadda). Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji read (a-wa-la yatadhakkaru al-insan) with a ya and a ta. "The lovers' places of visit have grown distant, so your pursuit of me, daughter of Makhram, has become hard on me."

He meant: your pursuit of her. On this passing over there are five opinions:

Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn al-Sumayfa, and Abu Raja read (nunahhi) with an unpointed ha' and a shadda. This verse is used as evidence by those who say that all creation will enter it, because rescue (najah) is the extraction of one who has fallen into a thing. This is reinforced by His words: ﴿And We will leave the wrongdoers therein﴾, and He did not say "We will admit them." One says "nadhara" and "natruku" (we leave) only of one who has already been in his place. Whoever says that passing over is for the disbelievers alone says: the meaning of this speech is: "We will bring out the God-conscious from among those who enter the Fire." By "the God-conscious" are meant those who avoided polytheism, and by "the wrongdoers" are meant the disbelievers. The meaning of His words ﴿on their knees﴾ (Maryam 19:68) has already been mentioned.

[p. 252] Allah's words: ﴿And man says﴾. The occasion of revelation of this verse: Ubayy ibn Khalaf took an old, decayed bone, began crumbling it in his hand and scattering it into the wind, and said: "Muhammad claims for you that Allah will resurrect us after we have become like this decayed bone." So this verse was revealed. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas. Ata narrated from Ibn Abbas that it was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

Allah's words: ﴿Shall I really be brought out alive?﴾ If it is asked: its apparent form is that of a question, so where is its answer? On this, Ibn al-Anbari mentions three answers:

The first: the apparent form of the speech is interrogative, but its meaning is one of denial and rejection. Its summary: "I am not going to be resurrected after death."

The second: when he asked this question about resurrection, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, answered him with His words: ﴿Does man not remember?﴾ So it contains the meaning of "Yes, you will be resurrected."

The third: the answer to the question of this disbeliever is in (Ya-Sin 36:78), at His words: ﴿And he strikes for Us a parable﴾, and it is not denied after the answer, because the whole Qur'an is like a single message, and the two surahs are Meccan.

Allah's words: ﴿Does man not remember?﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read yadhkuru with a fatha on the dhal and a shadda on the kaf. Nafi', Asim and Ibn Amir read (yadhkuru) with a sukun on the dhal and light (without shadda). Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji read (a-wa-la yatadhakkaru al-insan) with a ya and a ta. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and al-Hasan read (yadhkuru) with a ya and no ta, with a sukun on the dhal, light, and a damma on the kaf. The meaning: "Does this denier not remember his first creation, so that the beginning is taken as evidence for the return?"

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾, meaning: those who denied the resurrection, ﴿and the devils﴾, i.e., together with the devils, because every disbeliever is gathered with his devil in a chain. ﴿Then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees﴾ [p. 253]. Muqatil said: meaning, in Hell. For around something may be inside it: one says "the people sat around the house" when they sat inside it, encircling it. It was also said: they will crouch around it before they enter it.

As for His words ﴿on their knees (jithiyyan)﴾, al-Zajjaj said: it is the plural of jathin, like qa'id and qu'ud (sitter and sitters). It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. The original form has a damma on the jim, but it came with a kasra on it by assimilation to the kasra on the tha'.

The commentators have five opinions on its meaning:

The first: sitting, narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. The second: in groups, groups, also narrated from Ibn Abbas. On this view it is the plural of jathwa, which is a heap of earth and stones gathered together. The third: on their knees, said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Zajjaj. The fourth: standing, said by Abu Malik. The fifth: standing on their knees, said by al-Suddi, because of the narrowness of the place for them.

Allah's words: ﴿Then We will surely drag out from every sect﴾, i.e., We will take from every group, nation, and people of a religion, ﴿whichever of them was most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., the greatest of them in disobedience toward Him. The meaning: punishment begins with the most defiant, then the next most defiant, and with those greatest in crime and the leaders in evil. Al-Zajjaj said: regarding the nominative case of ayyuhum (whichever of them) there are three opinions:

The first: it is a fresh beginning, and "la-nanzi'anna" (We will surely drag out) has not governed anything. This is the view of Yunus.

The second: it is according to the sense of "those who are told to them: 'Which of them is most insolent toward the Most Merciful?'" This was said by al-Khalil and chosen by al-Zajjaj. He said: the interpretation is: "We will surely drag out the one who, because of his insolence..." It is said: "Which of these is most insolent?" And he recited a line [p. 254]:

"Indeed I spend the night away from the girl in a dwelling, so I spend the night neither troubled nor deprived."

The meaning: I spend the night like one of whom it is said: "He is neither troubled nor deprived."

The third: ayyuhum is built on a damma because it differs from its sisters. The meaning: "Which of them is the best?" The way it differs from its sisters is that you say "Strike whichever is best," but it is not good to say "Strike whoever is best" until you say "whoever is the best," and it is not good to say "Eat what is best" until you say "what is the best," nor "Take what is best" until you say "the one who is the best." So since "ma," "man," and "alladhi" differ from it, it was built on a damma. This was said by Sibawayh.

Allah's words: ﴿Then indeed We are most knowing of those most deserving of burning therein﴾. The meaning: the ones most deserving of burning therein are those who are most insolent, so they will be begun with before their followers. "Saliyyan" is in the accusative as a specification. It is said: "salia al-nar yaslaha" (he burned in the fire), when he entered it and endured its heat.

Allah's words: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾. There is an implied element in the speech; its estimate: "And there is none of you but he will pass over it."

Concerning who is intended by this address there are two opinions:

One: it is general concerning both the believer and the disbeliever. This is the view of the majority. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: this verse is for the disbelievers, but most of the narrations from him are like the first view. Ibn al-Anbari said: the reasoning for this is that when He said ﴿We will surely bring them﴾ and said ﴿whichever of them was most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾, the estimate was: "And there is none of them," so the kaf was replaced by the ha', as is done in His words: ﴿Indeed this was a reward for you﴾ (al-Insan 76:22), meaning "for them," because it refers back to His words ﴿and their Lord gave them to drink﴾ (al-Insan 76:21). A poet said:

"The lovers' places of visit have grown distant, so your pursuit of me, daughter of Makhram, has become hard on me."

He meant: your pursuit of her. On this passing over there are five opinions:

The first: it is entering. Jabir ibn Abd Allah narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Passing over is entering. Neither the righteous nor the wicked will remain who do not enter it. It will be cool and safe for the believer, as it was for Ibrahim, so much so that the Fire, or he said Hell, will cry out from their coolness." It was narrated from Ibn Abbas that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him about this verse, and he said to him: "As for you and me, we will enter it. So look: will Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bring us out of it or not?" He argued with His words: ﴿So He brought them to the Fire﴾ (Hud 11:98) and with His words: ﴿You and what you worship are fuel for Hell; you are going to it as passers-by﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:98). Abd Allah ibn Rawahah used to weep and say: "I have been told that I will pass over it, but I have not been told that I will come out from it." Al-Hasan al-Basri related that a man said to his brother: "O my brother, has it reached you that you will pass over the Fire?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Has it reached you that you will come out of it?" He said: "No." He said: "Then why laugh?" Khalid ibn Ma'dan said: when the people of Paradise enter Paradise they will say: "Did not our Lord promise us that we would pass over the Fire?" They will be told: "Yes, but you passed by it while it was extinguished."

Among those who held that it means entering are al-Hasan in one report, and Abu Malik. [p. 256] Objections have been raised against the proponents of this view on several grounds. Al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs say "I came to the land of such-and-such" and "I came to the water of such-and-such" when they approach it even if they do not enter, and from this is His words: ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan﴾ (al-Qasas 28:23). The decisive proof in this view is His words: ﴿Those will be kept far from it, they will not hear its faintest sound﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:101-102). Zuhayr said:

"When they came to the water, its pools blue, they set down the staves of the settled, encamped people."

That is, when they reached the water they stood over it.

I say: some of them have answered these arguments, saying: as for the first verse, when Musa stayed until he drew water and watered the sheep, his staying and his handling of it was as if he had entered. As for the other verse, it contains reports about the people of Paradise when they are in it, and then they will not hear its faintest sound. We have already related above from Khalid ibn Ma'dan that they pass by it and do not know it.

The second: passing over it means passing across it. This was said by Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah. Ibn Mas'ud said: people pass over the Fire, then they come out from it according to their deeds. The first of them will be like the flash of lightning, then like the wind, then like the running of a horse, [then like a rider on his mount], then like the tightening of the saddle, then like his walking.

The third: their passing over it means their presence at it. This was said by Ubayd ibn Umayr.

The fourth: the passing over of the Muslims means crossing the bridge, and the passing over of the polytheists means entering it. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: the believer's passing over it is what afflicts him of fever in this world. Uthman ibn al-Aswad narrated from Mujahid that he said: fever is every believer's share of the Fire. Then he recited: "And there is none of you but will pass over it." On this view, whoever among the Muslims has a fever has passed over it.

Allah's words: ﴿It is a decree binding upon your Lord﴾, meaning: the passing over, ﴿decided﴾. Hatm means making the judgment obligatory and cutting the matter off. The one decreed is the one Allah has decreed. The meaning: He made it binding and decreed it upon creation.

Allah's words: ﴿Then We will save those who were mindful of God﴾. Ibn Abbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn Yamur, Ibn Abi Layla, and Asim al-Jahdari read (thamma) with a fatha on the tha'. Al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read (nunji) with light pronunciation. Aisha, Abu Bahriyya, and Abu al-Jawza al-Rab'i read (thumma yunji) with a ya that is raised before the nun, light on the jim, and kasra. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Mijlaz, Ibn al-Sumayfa, and Abu Raja read (nunahhi) with an unpointed ha' and a shadda. Whoever says that passing over is for the disbelievers alone says: the meaning of this speech is: "We will bring out the God-conscious from among those who enter the Fire." By "the God-conscious" are meant those who avoided polytheism, and by "the wrongdoers" are meant the disbelievers. The meaning of His words ﴿on their knees﴾ (Maryam 19:68) has already been mentioned.

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 19, verses 73–74:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾, meaning the polytheists, ﴿Our verses﴾, meaning the Qur'an. [p. 258] ﴿Those who disbelieved said﴾, meaning the polytheists of Quraysh, ﴿to those who believed﴾, that is, to the poor among the believers, ﴿"Which of the two groups is better in position (maqaman) and finer in assembly (nadiyyan)?"﴾

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read *maqaman* with a fathah on the mim. Ibn Kathir read it with a dammah on the mim. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: *al-maqam* (the place of dwelling, the station) is a noun denoting the place of abode, whether the mim is read with a fathah or a dammah.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and finer in assembly (nadiyyan)﴾. *Al-nadiyy* and *al-nadi* (the gathering place, the assembly) mean the meeting place of a people and their gathering. Al-Farra' said: *al-nidiyy* and *al-nadi* are two dialectal forms. The meaning of the statement is: "Are we better, or are you?" So they boasted over them with their dwellings and their gatherings. Allah the Exalted answered them, saying: ﴿How many generations (qarn) before them did We destroy﴾. The meaning of *qarn* has already been explained in (al-An'am: 6), and we explained *athath* (furnishings, goods) in (al-Nahl: 80).

As for Allah's words ﴿and appearance (ri'yan)﴾: Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *ri'yan* with a hamzah between the ra' and the ya', on the pattern of *ri'an* (like *ri'an*, in the sense of sight or appearance). Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "sight" (manzaran), derived from *ra'aytu* (I saw).

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *riyyan* with a shaddah on the ya' and without a hamzah. Al-Zajjaj said: it has two interpretations. The first is that it has the same meaning as the first reading. The second is that it derives from *al-riyy* (satiety, fullness), so the meaning is: their appearance is replete with blessing, as if the bounty were visible upon them.

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', and Ibn Abi Surayj, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read *ziyyan* with a zay (with a dot), with a shaddah on the ya' and without a hamzah. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that their outward state is good (husn hay'atihim).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verse 75–76:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend [his term] for him﴾; that is, in disbelief and blindness regarding monotheism (tawhid). Al-Zajjaj said: this is in the form of a command, but its meaning is a report, and the meaning is that Allah, Exalted, made the recompense for his error to be that He leaves him in it. Ibn al-Anbari said: Allah addressed the Arabs in their own language, and they intend by mentioning a command to emphasize a report. One of them says: "If ʿAbd Allah visits us, let us honor him," intending emphasis and drawing attention to the fact that he binds himself to honor him. It is also permissible that the lam be the lam of supplication, in the sense of: "Say, O Muhammad: Whoever is in error, O Allah, extend for him in blessings an extension." The exegetes said: the meaning of Allah's extending for him is His giving him respite in his transgression. ﴿Until, when they see﴾, meaning: those whom He extended in error. He reported about them in the plural because the word "man" (whoever) is suitable for the plural. Then He mentioned what they are promised, saying: ﴿either the punishment﴾, meaning killing and captivity, ﴿or the Hour﴾, meaning the Resurrection and what they are promised therein of abiding forever in the Fire. ﴿So they will know who is worse in position﴾ in the Hereafter: is it they, or the believers? For the place of these is the Garden and the place of those is the Fire. And they will know through victory and killing who is "weaker in troops": their troops or the troops of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is a refutation of their saying: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance﴾. Concerning this there are five sayings:

One: Allah increases those who are guided through monotheism in faith. Two: He increases them in insight into their religion. Three: He increases them in faith by the increase of revelation, so that whenever a surah is revealed their faith increases. Four: He increases them in faith through the abrogating and the abrogated (al-nasikh wa al-mansukh). Five: Allah increases those who are guided by the abrogated in guidance through the abrogating. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that Allah, Exalted, makes their recompense that He increases them in certainty, just as the recompense of the disbeliever was made that He extends him in his error.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾. We have mentioned it in Surah al-Kahf (46). (p-260)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And better in return﴾. The "maradd" here is a verbal noun like "radd" (return), and the meaning is: better in return of reward to their doers, unlike the deeds of the disbelievers, which they lost, so they came to nothing.

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 19, verses 77–80:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

The first: al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated in their *Sahihs*, from the report of Masruq, from Khabbab [ibn al-Aratt], who said: "I was a *qayn* (that is, a blacksmith). I had a debt owed to me by al-As ibn Wa'il, so I came to him to demand it. He said: 'No, by God, I will not pay you until you disbelieve in Muhammad.' I said: 'No, by God, I will not disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ until you die and are then resurrected.' He said: 'When I die and am resurrected, I will come to you with wealth and children, and I will pay you then.' So this verse was revealed concerning him, up to His saying: ﴿alone﴾."

The second: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. This is related from al-Hasan, but the exegetes follow the first account.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿*walad*﴾ with a fatha on the waw. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿*wulad*﴾ with a damma on the waw. Al-Farra' said: "They are two dialects, like *'adam* and *'udm* (both meaning 'lack'). It is not used in the plural, though the Qays tribe makes *wulad* a plural and *walad* with a fatha a singular."

As for the disbeliever's claim that he would be given wealth and children, there are two views. The first: he meant in the Garden, according to your claim. The second: in this world. Ibn al-Anbari said: the implied sense of the verse is: "Do you consider him to be correct?" (p-261)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Has he looked into the unseen﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said in one report: "Has he known what is hidden from him, so that he knows whether he is in the Garden or not?" He said in another report: "Has he looked into the Preserved Tablet?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. There are three views on this:

First: "Has he said: 'There is no god but God,' so that He will have mercy on him for it?" This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: "Has he sent ahead a righteous deed, and so he hopes for it?" This was said by Qatadah.

Third: "Has a covenant been made with him that He will admit him into the Garden?" This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿No!﴾. That is: the matter is not as he claimed, that he will be given wealth and children. It is also permissible that the meaning of *kalla* is: he has not looked into the unseen, and he has not taken a covenant with God.

﴿We will record what he says﴾: that is, We will order the guardian angels (*hafazah*) to record his words against him, so that We may repay him for them.

﴿And We will extend for him an extension of punishment﴾: that is, We will make some of the punishment follow upon other punishment.

Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi and Abu Raja' al-Utaridi read ﴿*sayaktubu*﴾ and ﴿*yaritha-hu*﴾ with an open *ya'* (third person).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We will inherit from him what he says﴾. There are two views on this:

First: "We will inherit from him what he says he will have in the Garden, and We will give it to others among the Muslims." This was related from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and was preferred by al-Farra'.

Second: "We will inherit what he has of wealth and children, by destroying him and nullifying his dominion." This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah said it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "We will strip him of wealth and children and give them to others."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he will come to Us alone﴾: that is, without wealth and without children.

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 19, verses 77–80:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

The first: al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated in their *Sahihs*, from the report of Masruq, from Khabbab [ibn al-Aratt], who said: "I was a *qayn* (that is, a blacksmith). I had a debt owed to me by al-As ibn Wa'il, so I came to him to demand it. He said: 'No, by God, I will not pay you until you disbelieve in Muhammad.' I said: 'No, by God, I will not disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ until you die and are then resurrected.' He said: 'When I die and am resurrected, I will come to you with wealth and children, and I will pay you then.' So this verse was revealed concerning him, up to His saying: ﴿alone﴾."

The second: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. This is related from al-Hasan, but the exegetes follow the first account.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿*walad*﴾ with a fatha on the waw. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿*wulad*﴾ with a damma on the waw. Al-Farra' said: "They are two dialects, like *'adam* and *'udm* (both meaning 'lack'). It is not used in the plural, though the Qays tribe makes *wulad* a plural and *walad* with a fatha a singular."

As for the disbeliever's claim that he would be given wealth and children, there are two views. The first: he meant in the Garden, according to your claim. The second: in this world. Ibn al-Anbari said: the implied sense of the verse is: "Do you consider him to be correct?" (p-261)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Has he looked into the unseen﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said in one report: "Has he known what is hidden from him, so that he knows whether he is in the Garden or not?" He said in another report: "Has he looked into the Preserved Tablet?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. There are three views on this:

First: "Has he said: 'There is no god but God,' so that He will have mercy on him for it?" This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: "Has he sent ahead a righteous deed, and so he hopes for it?" This was said by Qatadah.

Third: "Has a covenant been made with him that He will admit him into the Garden?" This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿No!﴾. That is: the matter is not as he claimed, that he will be given wealth and children. It is also permissible that the meaning of *kalla* is: he has not looked into the unseen, and he has not taken a covenant with God.

﴿We will record what he says﴾: that is, We will order the guardian angels (*hafazah*) to record his words against him, so that We may repay him for them.

﴿And We will extend for him an extension of punishment﴾: that is, We will make some of the punishment follow upon other punishment.

Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi and Abu Raja' al-Utaridi read ﴿*sayaktubu*﴾ and ﴿*yaritha-hu*﴾ with an open *ya'* (third person).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We will inherit from him what he says﴾. There are two views on this:

First: "We will inherit from him what he says he will have in the Garden, and We will give it to others among the Muslims." This was related from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and was preferred by al-Farra'.

Second: "We will inherit what he has of wealth and children, by destroying him and nullifying his dominion." This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah said it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "We will strip him of wealth and children and give them to others."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he will come to Us alone﴾: that is, without wealth and without children.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verse 81–84:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they may be for them a source of honor﴾. That is, the polytheists, the worshippers of idols. Al-Farra' said: "That they may be for them intercessors in the Hereafter."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿No! They will reject their worship﴾. That is: the matter is not as they assumed. ﴿They will reject﴾, meaning the idols will deny the worship of the polytheists, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They did not used to worship us﴾ [al-Qasas: 63]; because they were inanimate objects that do not comprehend worship. ﴿And they will be against them﴾, meaning the idols will be against the polytheists, ﴿opponents﴾; that is, helpers against them on the Day of Resurrection, who will deny them and curse them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "Regarding the meaning of this sending there are two aspects.

One of them: We left the devils and the disbelievers to one another, and did not protect them from accepting from them.

The second, and it is the preferred one: We empowered them over them and assigned them to them because of their disbelief." ﴿Inciting them with incitement﴾; that is, agitating them with agitation until they mount the sins. Al-Farra' said: "They agitate them toward the sins and entice them to them." Ibn Faris said: "It is said: azzahu 'ala kadhā (he urged him upon such-and-such) when he incited him to it, and azzat al-qidr (the pot boiled over)."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So do not hasten against them﴾; that is, do not hasten in seeking their punishment. Some claimed that this is abrogated by the verse of the sword, but this is not correct. ﴿Indeed, We count for them a counting﴾. Regarding what is being counted there are three opinions:

One of them: it is their breaths. Ibn Abi Talha narrated it from Ibn Abbas, and Tawus and Muqatil said likewise. (p-263)

The second: it is the days, the nights, the months, the years, and the hours. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

The third: it is their deeds, said by Qutrub.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verses 85–87:

Allah's words, ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing﴾. Some said: this is connected to His words, ﴿and they will become opposed to them﴾ (19:82), so that ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing﴾ is its object. Others said: its implied sense is, "Mention to them the Day We gather the God-fearing," who are those who feared Allah by obeying Him and avoiding His disobedience.

Ibn Mas'ud and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read (يَوْمَ يَحْشُرُ) with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the shīn, and (وَيَسُوقُ) with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the sīn. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan al-Basri, Mu'adh al-Qari and Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji read (يَوْمَ يُحْشَرُ) with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the shīn, (الْمُتَّقُونَ) in the nominative, (وَيُسَاقُ) with an alif and a damma on the yā', and (الْمُجْرِمُونَ) with a wāw in the nominative.

Al-Wafd (the delegations) is the plural of wāfid, like rakb and rākib, and ṣaḥb and ṣāḥib. Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrimah and al-Farra' said: al-Wafd means the riders. Ibn al-Anbari said: among the Arabs, al-rukbān means the camel-riders.

There are two opinions about the time of this gathering:

One: it is from their graves to the Most Merciful. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The other: it is after the reckoning. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Allah's words, ﴿and We will drive the guilty﴾, meaning the disbelievers, ﴿to Hell in thirst﴾ (wirdan). Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah and al-Hasan said: thirsty. [p. 264] Abu 'Ubayda said: al-wird is the verbal noun of al-wurūd (coming to water). Ibn Qutayba said: al-wird is a group who come to the water, meaning that they are thirsty, because only one who is thirsty comes to water. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of His words, ﴿wirdan﴾, is "those coming (to water)."

Allah's words, ﴿they will not possess intercession﴾; that is, they will not intercede, nor will intercession be made for them.

Allah's words, ﴿except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible for man (مَن, "those who") to be in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for the wāw and nūn of the verb, so the meaning is: no one possesses intercession except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative position as an exception that is not from the first part, so the meaning is: the guilty do not possess intercession; then He said, ﴿except﴾ in the sense of (لَكِنْ, "but"), ﴿those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾, for they possess intercession. The covenant here is the affirmation of Allah's oneness and faith in Him. Ibn al-Anbari said: the explanation of "covenant" (ʿahd) in the language is: a prior commitment to a matter that is known and kept, from your saying, "I knew (ʿahidtu) so-and-so in the place," meaning I recognised him and witnessed him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verses 85–87:

Allah's words, ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing﴾. Some said: this is connected to His words, ﴿and they will become opposed to them﴾ (19:82), so that ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing﴾ is its object. Others said: its implied sense is, "Mention to them the Day We gather the God-fearing," who are those who feared Allah by obeying Him and avoiding His disobedience.

Ibn Mas'ud and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read (يَوْمَ يَحْشُرُ) with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the shīn, and (وَيَسُوقُ) with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the sīn. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan al-Basri, Mu'adh al-Qari and Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji read (يَوْمَ يُحْشَرُ) with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the shīn, (الْمُتَّقُونَ) in the nominative, (وَيُسَاقُ) with an alif and a damma on the yā', and (الْمُجْرِمُونَ) with a wāw in the nominative.

Al-Wafd (the delegations) is the plural of wāfid, like rakb and rākib, and ṣaḥb and ṣāḥib. Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrimah and al-Farra' said: al-Wafd means the riders. Ibn al-Anbari said: among the Arabs, al-rukbān means the camel-riders.

There are two opinions about the time of this gathering:

One: it is from their graves to the Most Merciful. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The other: it is after the reckoning. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Allah's words, ﴿and We will drive the guilty﴾, meaning the disbelievers, ﴿to Hell in thirst﴾ (wirdan). Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah and al-Hasan said: thirsty. [p. 264] Abu 'Ubayda said: al-wird is the verbal noun of al-wurūd (coming to water). Ibn Qutayba said: al-wird is a group who come to the water, meaning that they are thirsty, because only one who is thirsty comes to water. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of His words, ﴿wirdan﴾, is "those coming (to water)."

Allah's words, ﴿they will not possess intercession﴾; that is, they will not intercede, nor will intercession be made for them.

Allah's words, ﴿except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible for man (مَن, "those who") to be in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for the wāw and nūn of the verb, so the meaning is: no one possesses intercession except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (*Zad al-Masir*) on Surah 19, verses 88–95:

Allah's words: ﴿They say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ This refers to the Jews and the Christians, and to those among the polytheists who claimed that the angels are the daughters of Allah. ﴿Indeed you have produced a thing monstrous.﴾ That is, a great thing of disbelief. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-idd* and *al-nukr* both mean a matter that has reached its utmost greatness.

Allah's words: ﴿The heavens are about to be torn apart (yatafattarna) from it.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read *takadu* (تَكادُ) with the *ta'* (تاء). Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read *yakadu* (يَكادُ) with the *ya'* (ياء). Both of them, together, read *yatafattarna* (يَتَفَطَّرْنَ) with *ya'* and with the *ta'* having a shadda on the *ta'* (the *tha* is doubled). Ibn Kathir and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, agreed with them on *yatafattarna*. Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read *yanfatirna* (يَنْفَطِرْنَ) with the *nun*. Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir read in Maryam like Abu 'Amr, and in *'Asaqa* (42:5) like Ibn Kathir. The meaning of *yatafattarna minhu* is that they nearly split apart from it, from your saying. Ibn Qutaybah said: Allah's words ﴿*hadda*﴾ mean: falling down.

Allah's words: ﴿that they ascribe (da'aw) to the Most Merciful a son.﴾ Al-Farra' said: it means "from (an) da'aw" and "because (li-an) da'aw." Abu 'Ubaydah said: its meaning is "that they made," and it is not from calling out aloud. He recited:

Many a one you call a counselor, though if he is absent you will find him one whose heart is not sincere.

Allah's words: ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ That is: it is not proper for Him, nor suitable for Him, to take a son, because a son requires similarity of nature, and everyone who takes a son takes him from his own kind. Allah, the Exalted, is far above sharing a nature with anything or anything sharing a nature with Him, so taking a son is impossible with respect to Him. ﴿There is not any within the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿humbled and submissive.﴾ The meaning is that 'Isa, 'Uzair, and the angels are servants to Him. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: In this there is an indication that if a father buys his son, the father's ownership over him does not remain, and he is freed by the act of purchase itself, because Allah, the Exalted, negated sonship on account of servitude, and this indicates that sonship and slavery cannot coexist.

Allah's words: ﴿He has enumerated them and counted them precisely.﴾ That is: He knows their number. ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾ without wealth and without any helper to protect him, so the total of all of them, despite their multitude, is not hidden from Him.

If it is said: For what reason did He use the singular in "al-Rahman" and "atihi," and the plural in the pronoun referring to them in "ahsahum" and "addahum"?

The answer: every word has a singular form and a plural interpretation. The singular is taken according to the wording, and the plural is directed toward the meaning.

Allah, the Exalted, is far above sharing a nature with anything or anything sharing a nature with Him, so taking a son is impossible with respect to Him. ﴿There is not any within the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿humbled and submissive.﴾ The meaning is that 'Isa, 'Uzair, and the angels are servants to Him. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: In this there is an indication that if a father buys his son, the father's ownership over him does not remain, and he is freed by the act of purchase itself, because Allah, the Exalted, negated sonship on account of servitude, and this indicates that sonship and slavery cannot coexist.

Allah's words: ﴿He has enumerated them and counted them precisely.﴾ That is: He knows their number. ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾ without wealth and without any helper to protect him, so the total of all of them, despite their multitude, is not hidden from Him.

If it is said: For what reason did He use the singular in "al-Rahman" and "atihi," and the plural in the pronoun referring to them in "ahsahum" and "addahum"?

The answer: every word has a singular form and a plural interpretation. The singular is taken according to the wording, and the plural is directed toward the meaning.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (*Zad al-Masir*) on Surah 19, verses 88–95:

Allah's words: ﴿They say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ This refers to the Jews and the Christians, and to those among the polytheists who claimed that the angels are the daughters of Allah. ﴿Indeed you have produced a thing monstrous.﴾ That is, a great thing of disbelief. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-idd* and *al-nukr* both mean a matter that has reached its utmost greatness.

Allah's words: ﴿The heavens are about to be torn apart (yatafattarna) from it.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read *takadu* (تَكادُ) with the *ta'* (تاء). Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read *yakadu* (يَكادُ) with the *ya'* (ياء). Both of them, together, read *yatafattarna* (يَتَفَطَّرْنَ) with *ya'* and with the *ta'* having a shadda on the *ta'* (the *tha* is doubled). Ibn Kathir and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, agreed with them on *yatafattarna*. Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read *yanfatirna* (يَنْفَطِرْنَ) with the *nun*. Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir read in Maryam like Abu 'Amr, and in *'Asaqa* (42:5) like Ibn Kathir. The meaning of *yatafattarna minhu* is that they nearly split apart from it, from your saying. Ibn Qutaybah said: Allah's words ﴿*hadda*﴾ mean: falling down.

Allah's words: ﴿that they ascribe (da'aw) to the Most Merciful a son.﴾ Al-Farra' said: it means "from (an) da'aw" and "because (li-an) da'aw." Abu 'Ubaydah said: its meaning is "that they made," and it is not from calling out aloud. He recited:

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 19, verses 96–98:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful will bestow upon them affection﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning ʿAli, peace be upon him, and he said: its meaning is: He loves them and makes them beloved to the believers. Qatada said: He places affection for them in the hearts of the believers. Among this is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "When Allah loves a servant, He says: O Jibril, I love so-and-so, so love him. Then Jibril calls out in the heavens: Indeed Allah loves so-and-so, so love him. Then his love is cast upon the people of the earth, and he is loved." And he mentioned the same concerning hatred. Harim ibn Hayyan said: No servant turns his heart toward Allah, mighty and majestic, except that Allah, mighty and majestic, turns the hearts of the people of faith toward him, until He grants him their affection and their mercy.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue﴾. He means: the Qur'an. Ibn Qutayba said: That is, We made it easy and sent it down in your language. And ﴿al-Ludd﴾ is the plural of ﴿alladd﴾, which is the stubborn adversary, the contentious one.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them? Do you perceive any of them, or hear from them a whisper?﴾ This is a warning to the disbelievers of Makkah. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, do you see? It is said: "Did you perceive your companion?", meaning: did you see him? Al-rikz is a faint sound. Ibn Qutayba said: a sound that is not understood. Abu Salih said: a movement. [And Allah knows best.]
